For strength training to be effective, there are a few simple criteria you need to meet, according to Dr Schoenfeld.
Firstly, consistency is key. For the minimum effective dose, aim for two weekly workouts on non-consecutive days, every week.
Secondly, once you have fine-tuned your technique using lighter weights, your workouts need to be challenging. If the body is not challenged, it has no reason to change and adapt in the ways we want – more muscle, stronger tissues, myriad better health markers.
“If you’re lifting a weight, and at the end of your set you could do 10 more repetitions with the weight you’re using, you’re not really going to see much in the way of benefits,” says Dr Schoenfeld. “The last few repetitions [of each set] need to be difficult to complete.”
And finally, in each of your sessions, he recommends hitting every major muscle group for a full-body workout. (You can find an example of how to do this with just a pair of dumbbells below.)
If you meet these three conditions, and you give your body the fuel and recovery it needs, “you can produce really large improvements in overall strength, overall health, appearance and other factors too,” Dr Schoenfeld says.
Read more: Scared exercise will injure you? These rules make any routine safe
Why it’s never too late to begin strength training
In 1990, researchers recruited 10 frail residents of a chronic care hospital, each aged 90 or above. They were put through eight weeks of “high-intensity resistance training” – in this case, machine leg extensions.
By the end of the study, two of the 10 subjects no longer used walking sticks to walk, while another regained the ability to rise from his chair without support from his arms. Gait speed, mobility and strength also shot up, while no injuries or adverse impacts on the heart and lungs were reported.
If you start lifting when you’re younger, you can basically maintain your muscle throughout your life
“It’s never too late to start,” says Dr Schoenfeld. “Many people would say the leg extension is one of the least functional exercises – it’s single-joint and uses a machine – but it allowed multiple people to walk without their canes in a very short period of time.”
He caveats this with the message that, the earlier you start strength training, the better.
“This is because there is a progressive loss of muscle over time,” Dr Schoenfeld explains. “Once you get into your thirties and forties, you start to lose about a half per cent of muscle per year if you’re sedentary. This goes up exponentially as you get into your fifties and sixties, and then your seventies and eighties, because you become less and less active.
“But if you start lifting when you’re younger, you can basically maintain your muscle throughout your life.”
![A couple of 20-minute dumbbell workouts each week can transform your health and fitness, according to muscle expert Dr Brad Schoenfeld](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/15/41/AdobeStock_417863469.jpeg)
For many reasons, exercise can be easier to pick up when you are younger. And, due to various biological factors, a 20-year-old might have a higher fitness ceiling than someone in their 50s, 60s, 70s and beyond. But a fit and active person in the latter group will likely trounce a sedentary 20-something on many health and fitness fronts.
“We see over and over in studies on the topic that older individuals see these massive benefits from strength training – again, in a very short period of time,” Dr Schoenfeld says. “If you just stick with it, training on a couple of days a week for a couple of months, you’ll see huge benefits.”
His group conducted a meta-analysis into the effects of strength training on people aged 75 and above. They uncovered significant strength and muscle benefits, which naturally carry over to mobility, functionality and independence.
In other words: strength training is not the fountain of youth, but it’s one of the closest things we have, and it’s more accessible than many would have you believe.
Read more: Expert coach shares five kettlebell workouts to get you in ‘the shape of your life’
Feel the fear – but do it anyway
The other major obstacle standing between people and regular strength training is trepidation. They fear injury, or believe they are not flexible enough to perform any of the exercises.
But there is a form of strength training that is suitable for everyone. Take the nonagenarians in the study above. Several could not stand up from their chairs unassisted, so squats were out of the question as a leg-strengthening exercise. Instead, they used a leg extension machine to bolster the leg muscles, and significant benefits soon followed.
If you do not have access to a gym, you could simply sit in a chair then use your hands to support you as you stand up again, and repeat this for several repetitions. If this feels challenging to you, it will have the wanted impact on your fitness levels.
“People think that, when you lift, you have to lift really heavy weights,” Dr Schoenfeld explains. “But in research from our lab we’ve consistently seen that moderate to lighter loads can provide very similar benefits.
“Heavy loads do carry risk, and as people get older they tend to have osteoarthritis and other joint-related issues. But whatever load you’re lifting, if you’re challenging your muscles at the end of the set, you will get very good results.”
summary: Strength training offers profound health and longevity benefits, yet many avoid it due to perceived lack of time or fear of injury. According to exercise science expert Dr Brad Schoenfeld, just two 20- to 30-minute sessions per week targeting major muscle groups can yield major improvements in health and fitness. Furthermore, research shows it is never too late to begin, with older adults—including those in their 90s—experiencing rapid and significant gains in strength, mobility, and independence.
key_points: Just two 20- to 30-minute strength training sessions a week are enough to significantly improve health and reduce chronic disease risk.
Effective workouts require consistency (non-consecutive days), challenging effort where the final repetitions are difficult, and full-body engagement.
Studies on individuals aged 90 and above demonstrate that strength training can rapidly improve mobility, gait speed, and independence.
Moderate to lighter loads can provide benefits similar to heavy lifting as long as the muscles are adequately challenged at the end of a set.

title: Woman says she lay on hospital floor in 'excruciating' pain for seven hours
author: Imogen Barber
content:
A woman claims she was left lying on a hospital floor for seven hours in "excruciating" pain.
Tammi Radcliffe, 31, from south Cumbria, said she was forced to wait for treatment after being taken to Royal Preston Hospital on August 15 by ambulance.
She began experiencing sudden stomach pain while shopping at Asda and said the pain became so severe that she nearly passed out.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
Ms Radcliffe said: "I've never felt pain like that in my life and I'm the kind of a person to downplay things, and I'm definitely one to mask my pain in public.
"But there was no hiding it, I was uncontrollable, just crying and doubled over in pain in the waiting room begging for pain relief."
The administrator initially believed her symptoms were caused by trapped wind.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
She said: "I'd had cramps all morning but I just passed it off as trapped wind.
"I thought I’d go to ASDA to get myself some paracetamol and some Rennies or Windies or something, but as I was walking around, the pain just became so severe.
"I started to lose my vision, the light faded and I felt super lightheaded - like I was about to pass out.
"So I went to the pharmacy, and told them that I was on my own and didn’t know what else to do.
"They sat me down, and they ended up calling an ambulance for me and then sat with me and waited as the pain was just becoming more severe and I was crying."
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
Paramedics gave her IV paracetamol before taking her to hospital, where she arrived at 4pm and was initially triaged.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
However, she said she was not seen by a doctor for seven hours and was left lying on the floor in the waiting room.
Her husband, Corey, said: "I asked for more pain medication at least six times in the space of two hours and sometimes they didn’t even acknowledge us asking.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
"I was asking for her to be reassessed and re-triaged but all we got in response was that she had already been triaged so go and sit down because she is where she needs to be.
"Tammi was so exhausted and unwell that she ended up lying on the floor of the A&E department under a wheelchair to block out the bright hospital lights.
"We were there for hours before her temperature was actually checked.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
"By then it had reached 39 degrees and she was shaking."
He said that despite her high temperature and apparent distress, she was not given stronger medication until 9pm.
Blood tests later revealed raised infection markers.
Mr Radcliffe said: "Despite how unwell she was, it took about seven hours for her to see a doctor."
She was finally seen by a doctor at 11pm and prescribed IV antibiotics, but did not receive them until 2.30am.
Ms Radcliffe said she was moved to the gynaecology ward around 3am and discharged later that day without a diagnosis.
She said: "Doctors weren't 100% sure what was causing my pain because they have to do swabs and an ultrasound scan.
  Tammi Radcliffe was left to lay on a hospital floor for seven hours in excruciating pain. (Image: Corey Radcliffe / SWNS)
"We haven't actually got any formal diagnosis currently, and we had to wait four days for the scan which is pretty hard considering it's an emergency situation."
Tammi is still suffering extreme abdominal and pelvic pain.
A Lancashire Teaching Hospitals spokesperson said: "We would always encourage any patients or relatives who have concerns about their care to raise these with the clinical teams treating them at the time so, where possible, these can be resolved in real time.
"Where this is not possible, or where patients feel their concerns were not addressed, we would encourage them to get in touch with our Patient Experience and PALS team so that we can fully explore what happened and why and adopt any potential learning.
"In this instance, we are in direct contact with the family and are sorry that they have concerns about some aspects of the care received.
"We will fully investigate the issues the family have raised through our formal complaints process and respond directly back to them."
summary: Tammi Radcliffe, 31, claims she was left lying on the floor of the Royal Preston Hospital waiting room for seven hours in excruciating abdominal pain. An ambulance was called after she nearly passed out while shopping at Asda on August 15. She was eventually seen by a doctor, prescribed IV antibiotics, and later discharged without a formal diagnosis.
key_points: Tammi Radcliffe experienced sudden, severe stomach pain while shopping at Asda and was taken to Royal Preston Hospital by ambulance.
She stated she was left lying on the A&E waiting room floor for seven hours and had to wait until 11pm to see a doctor.
Her husband requested pain medication multiple times and reported that her temperature eventually reached 39 degrees.
She was discharged without a formal diagnosis and is still suffering from extreme abdominal and pelvic pain.
Lancashire Teaching Hospitals stated they are in direct contact with the family and will fully investigate the issues raised through their formal complaints process.

title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
author: Rachel Savage
content:
Every day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends.
“More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.”
![A health worker wearing full protective gear raises their hands in the air as another sprays them with disinfectant](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3fd347c389a8a1cc87d1169018d98aebc87a31a0/0_0_5500_3468/master/5500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.”
That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid.
“I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses.
Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.”
![A health worker holds a white boot by the sole next to other upturned boots on poles and rods](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/35be58a45cb94539e3e75341116e73665d21dc19/0_0_5821_3881/master/5821.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Unpaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.
More than 2,500 people have now died in the outbreak, which is spreading exponentially in an area larger than France, the senior UN Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, said on Friday. Speaking on a video call from Bunia, Harneis called for more aid, saying the existing pool of funds would run out within weeks. He said 160 healthcare workers had fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them had died.
“The outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response,” he added. “And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”
The World Health Organization estimates that the outbreak is on course to exceed west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest ever globally. In the previous outbreak, more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.
![Two health workers tend to a man lying on a bed as a woman looks on through a transparent protective sheet](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/aadd6ce13708a2d40a5cac067d627efa606ea37b/0_0_8256_5504/master/8256.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The infections in DRC are of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for the strain, but trials for both are under way.
Bolombi said he was working seven days a week, with barely any time to see his family, as the outbreak was getting worse. “Logistics have improved compared to the early days of the response, but this is still not enough, as needs are growing as the disease progresses,” he said.
Despite the enormous challenges and lack of renumeration, Kabundo expressed pride that there had been “a large number of recoveries” at the Elikya treatment centre. “This progress must be highlighted, but it is no excuse to rest on our laurels,” she said.
The Congolese health ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
![A long line of people queue to be tested by health workers sitting at tables next to a river](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/421ad51e10136ff59b5321189be36b661cc96525/0_0_3811_2541/master/3811.jpg?width=465&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads between humans via direct contact with the organs, blood or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies. It can also be spread through contact with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding or clothing.
Initial symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headaches and a sore throat. These progress to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.
Widespread mistrust and misinformation have resulted in people with the virus not attending health centres for treatment until it is too late, as well as attacks on health facilities and ambulances.
Dr Eddy Kambale Kahandukya, a deputy medical coordinator for the charity Médicins Sans Frontières in the DRC, said: “The lack of community engagement remains a major challenge in breaking this chain of transmission … For example, patients who suspect they have symptoms and are awaiting laboratory results seek refuge within the community and end up creating new clusters that further fuel the spread of the epidemic.”
![Three men in protective gear lower a coffin into the ground as mourners stand around the grave](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c8b1e016630f3d31117f907f46388388f4f38340/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Fear was a big driver of the lack of trust in the authorities’ response to Ebola, said Manon Dumortier, an emergency coordinator in Bunia for the aid group Mercy Corps.
“It’s scary, right? … Suddenly there are so many people dying and you don’t know what it is about,” she said. “People are just disappearing, going to health centres and you cannot even see them before they are being buried. This is just raising a lot of speculation and rumours.”
The WHO declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern in May, but later said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier in February.
The virus has spread to six of the DRC’s 26 provinces, concentrated in the country’s north-east. More than 4,200 of the confirmed cases are in Ituri, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths, all in the capital, Kampala. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.
summary: Frontline healthcare workers responding to an exponentially spreading Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are facing severe stress and missing their wages. The outbreak, which has caused over 2,500 deaths, is being hampered by unpaid wages, misinformation, community mistrust, and infrastructure deficits. Officials warn that funds are running out and the epidemic is growing faster than the medical response.
key_points: Frontline workers like nurses and hygiene staff are working without full pay, prompting protests and strikes.
More than 2,500 people have died in the DRC outbreak, with 160 healthcare workers infected and 43 of them dying.
The UN reports that existing funds will run out within weeks as the outbreak outpaces the current medical response.
Community mistrust, misinformation, and a lack of engagement are major challenges hampering efforts to break the chain of transmission.
The WHO estimates that the current outbreak is on course to exceed the 2014-16 west African Ebola outbreak as the biggest globally.

title: Prostate cancer cases surge by 100,000 in six years
author: Laura Donnelly
content:
The Department of Health has insisted that this did not amount to a right to a test, but simply a right to ask for one, saying the final decision was always intended to rest with the GP.
However, ministers representing successive governments have repeatedly described such a right.
In 2019, Steve Brine, the then public health minister, told the Commons: “Men over 50 have the right to be given a PSA test free on the NHS once they have discussed the advantages and disadvantages with their GP.”
He added: “The PCRMP [Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme] makes that very clear to GPs, and, having discussed the pros and cons, no one over 50 should be told ‘No’.”
The Telegraph is campaigning for the rollout of targeted screening, with PSA tests offered to black men, those with a family history of prostate cancer and those carrying other high-risk genes.
The number of men seeking tests has risen in recent years after a series of high-profile figures spoke publicly about their experiences of the disease, including Sir Stephen Fry and Bill Turnbull, the broadcaster.
Experts have noted a “staggering” rise in men seeking checks since Sir Chris revealed his terminal diagnosis in 2024.
The six-time Olympic cycling gold medallist is among those calling for screening to be rolled out so that men at high risk of the disease are offered checks.
summary: The Department of Health has clarified that men over 50 have the right to ask a GP for a PSA test rather than a guaranteed right to the test itself, despite ministers previously describing it as a right. Meanwhile, the number of men seeking prostate cancer checks has surged significantly in recent years. This increase has been driven by high-profile figures, including Sir Stephen Fry, Bill Turnbull, and Sir Chris Hoy, speaking publicly about their diagnoses.
key_points: The Department of Health states men over 50 have the right to ask for a PSA test, while GPs retain the final decision.
Successive government ministers have previously described the policy as a direct right to a free NHS PSA test after discussion.
The Telegraph is campaigning for targeted prostate cancer screening for high-risk groups.
High-profile figures sharing their diagnoses have driven a surge in men seeking checks.

title: Nutrition experts think they've solved vegan cheese's biggest flaw | BBC Science Focus Magazine
author: Ling Thomas; Dr Emma Davies
content:
Sales of dairy cheese are booming, with a huge demand for all things protein and increasing numbers of artisan cheese fanatics.
But plant-based vegan cheeses are becoming less popular because many are labelled as ultra-processed, with ingredients such as starches, gums, oils, colourings and flavourings.
However, some people still prefer a vegan alternative, concerned that cows release large volumes of the greenhouse gas methane to the atmosphere as they munch grass.
It’s very difficult to replicate the complex flavours and textures of traditional cheeses, and therefore most dairy-free products are imitations of mild cheddar, mozzarella and soft cheese.
Vegan cheeses often mainly comprise oil and starch with low to no levels of protein. Higher protein versions contain nuts or legumes such as lentils and chickpeas.
Some companies have found ways to use genetically engineered yeast, bacteria or fungi to produce copies of the casein proteins found in cow’s milk.
These proteins self-assemble to form tiny spherical structures called micelles, which play a key role in cheese’s structure and stretchiness. The non-dairy caseins can be used first to make milk and then cheese.
Vegan cheeses generally need very high concentrations of fat to create a product that can be sliced and melted. Coconut oil and palm oil are the most common types, both of which contain high levels of saturated fat.
![](https://www.sciencefocus.com/resources/content/6ab86ca8-b028-4715-93c8-27c92ae62f2a/d1f7a076-196c-4d35-bf8c-37319ffd53e6/e4604ca3-0b8d-4ec7-ba08-487fec258a16/Cheese.jpg?preview=false&platform=WEB&deviceId=96e0c4f5-f4d4-421b-a151-a89663bc66d6)
Scientists continue to innovate to create better-tasting, healthier vegan cheeses. A team at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh recently developed a way to create a meltable product using unsaturated sunflower oil or rapeseed oil.
They add molecules called oleogelators, which include waxes or proteins, to liquid oil to create a three-dimensional gel structure that behaves like a solid fat and is better at oozily melting than cheeses formed from coconut or palm oil.
In another recent development, scientists at the University of Arkansas, US, reported that waste products from rice milling could be good for making protein-packed vegan cheese.
They analysed proteins from brown rice, broken kernels and rice bran before combining them with coconut oil and corn starch to make a cheese with around 12 per cent protein.
Each protein fraction has different characteristics. In tests, cheese from brown rice protein had a firmer texture, whereas rice kernel proteins gave the most meltable cheese.
Elsewhere, microalgae, tiny organisms found in water, offer a tangy alternative. Microalgae can grow in big vats called bioreactors, fuelled by light and carbon dioxide.
One option is to make a microalgae protein flour and homogenise it with water to make a kind of milk.
The microalgae are an excellent source of amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants. Products made with them are reported to have a satisfyingly savoury taste known as umami.
So, while dairy cheese makers will always provide premium products for aficionados, vegan alternatives continue to get healthier and more like the real thing.
This article is an answer to the question (asked by Wendy Copsey, Lichfield) 'What is the future of cheese?'
To submit your questions, email us at questions@sciencefocus.com, or message our Facebook, X, or Instagram pages (don't forget to include your name and location).
Check out our ultimate fun facts page for more mind-blowing science
Read more:
summary: Plant-based vegan cheeses have faced declining popularity and criticism for being ultra-processed with low protein content. However, scientists are innovating with new ingredients and techniques, such as using oleogelators with unsaturated oils, rice milling waste, and microalgae. These advancements aim to improve the nutritional profile, texture, meltability, and flavor of vegan cheese alternatives.
key_points: Vegan cheeses often suffer from being labeled as ultra-processed and frequently lack protein while containing high levels of saturated fats like coconut or palm oil.
Researchers at Heriot-Watt University developed a meltable vegan cheese using unsaturated oils and oleogelators instead of saturated fats.
Scientists at the University of Arkansas created a protein-packed vegan cheese using waste products from rice milling.
Microalgae are being explored as a nutrient-rich ingredient that provides a savory umami taste for dairy alternatives.

title: DHSC sets out updated guidance on when GPs should offer PSA testing
author: Anna Colivicchi
content:
DHSC sets out updated guidance on when GPs should offer PSA testing
![DHSC sets out updated guidance on when GPs should offer PSA testing DHSC sets out updated guidance on when GPs should offer PSA testing](https://www.pulsetoday.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/c_files/web/y/r/u/GettyImages-675362328-scaled-e1673626665419-570x380.jpg) 
PSA blood tests should not be routinely offered on the NHS if a man does not have symptoms or have a BRCA2 gene variant, updated guidance to GPs has stated.
It follows recommendations from the National Screening Committee (NSC) in June for a targeted screening programme to be introduced.
After a review of the evidence and consultation period, the NSC advised against whole-population routine NHS prostate cancer screening – recommending instead a targeted screening programme involving PSA testing every two years for men aged 45 to 61 who have a pathogenic BRCA2 variant with a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate cancer.
In a letter setting out the current guidance, seen by Pulse, the Department of Health and Social Care said the previous Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme had been withdrawn, and GPs should refer to guidance in NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries when discussing the risks and benefits of the PSA test with patients.
The guidance no longer references men over 50 being at high risk because age is one factor in assessing risk but should not be the only consideration, the letter said.
It said: ‘If a patient is worried about prostate cancer, then they can ask their GP about having a PSA test.
‘As the health professional, the GP will consider the patient’s cancer risk to help with reaching a judgement on whether undertaking a PSA test is the right option for the patient, whilst clearly laying out to the patient the pros and cons associated with doing so.’
There is no change to the symptomatic pathway, the letter noted, and PSA testing should continue to be used in men presenting with symptoms.
And existing advice on access to genetic testing through the National Genomic Test Directories also remains the same.
DHSC said that to support GPs in implementing the updated policy, it is working with Cancer Research UK ‘to see if interim advice can be developed’ to support GPs in taking a decision when they are approached by asymptomatic men ‘who are concerned about family history’.
A group co-chaired by the RCGP and UK Cancer Genetics Group will bring together primary care clinicians, urologists and geneticists to ‘consider an appropriate way forward’.
In stage 2 of the TRANSFORM trial, funded by Prostate Cancer UK and the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) to test the best ways to detect prostate cancer earlier, all eligible Black men – aged 45 to 74, who have not had a PSA test or prostate MRI scan in the last five years – will be invited to take part. This is likely to start in 2028 with invitations sent out over a few years.
The letter added: ‘Some men may prefer to have a PSA test now rather than the chance of participating in the trial in the future. They should speak to their GP who will help them to understand the pros and cons of testing.’
The updated guidance had caused some newspapers and commentators to state that men had lost the right to a prostate cancer test and it was a step backwards.
But the DHSC said to suggest there had been a change in policy was ‘inaccurate and irresponsible’.
A spokesperson said: ‘There has been no change in policy whatsoever, and any suggestion otherwise is both inaccurate and irresponsible.
‘Every man still has the right to ask their GP for a PSA test, and it remains the case that the final decision rests with GPs. All this letter does is tell GPs and others where to find the most up to date guidance.
‘NHS advice remains that any man with prostate cancer symptoms should get themselves checked and should expect to be referred for a PSA test. Men who are concerned about prostate cancer but don’t have any symptoms should speak to their GP, who will help decide the right option for the patient.’
RCGP president Professor Victoria Tzortziou Brown said that GPs want to diagnose prostate cancer as early as possible, while also ‘protecting patients from unnecessary investigations and treatment’.
She said: ‘Men who have symptoms or are concerned about their risk of prostate cancer should speak to their GP, and those asking about a PSA test should have the opportunity to discuss whether testing is appropriate for them.
‘For men without symptoms, routine population PSA screening is not currently recommended, based on the evidence about the balance of potential benefits and harms. Decisions about PSA testing should be informed by national screening and clinical guidance, alongside the GP’s professional judgement and an individual discussion with the patient about their circumstances, risk factors and preferences.
‘The RCGP is also co-chairing an expert advisory group, bringing together GPs, urologists and geneticists, to inform the development of guidance to support conversations about PSA testing with asymptomatic men who have a family history of prostate cancer.
‘The PSA test is not perfect, which is why these conversations are important, and we welcome ongoing research, including the TRANSFORM trial, into more accurate ways to detect prostate cancer early.’
Visit Pulse Reference for details on 140 symptoms, including easily searchable symptoms and categories, offering you a free platform to check symptoms and receive potential diagnoses during consultations.

summary: The Department of Health and Social Care has issued updated guidance stating that PSA blood tests should not be routinely offered on the NHS to asymptomatic men without a BRCA2 gene variant. Following recommendations from the National Screening Committee, whole-population routine screening is not recommended, though men still retain the right to discuss PSA testing and its pros and cons with their GPs. The DHSC emphasized that there has been no change in policy regarding a man's right to request a test from their doctor.
key_points: PSA blood tests should not be routinely offered on the NHS to men without symptoms or a BRCA2 gene variant.

The National Screening Committee recommended against whole-population routine screening, favoring targeted screening for men aged 45 to 61 with a pathogenic BRCA2 variant and a relevant family history.
Men without symptoms retain the right to ask their GP for a PSA test, and the final decision on testing rests with the GP after discussing pros and cons.
The symptomatic pathway remains unchanged, and PSA testing should continue for men presenting with symptoms.

title: South East farmers urged to vaccinate animals against bluetongue
author: Cash Murphy
content:
![A black and white cow is pictured looking directly at the camera. It is standing in a green field and a few other cows and tree-covered hills can be seen in the background. The sky is blue with white fluffy clouds.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/924/cpsprodpb/1046/live/48c08be0-8cba-11f1-b49b-bb9fc846a015.png)
There have been more than 500 cases of potentially fatal bluetongue in the UK, according to the latest government figures
- Published
Farmers across the South East must vaccinate their animals against the potentially fatal bluetongue "as soon as possible", the National Farmers' Union (NFU) has said.
According to government figures published on Thursday,, external there have now been 517 cases of the virus in the UK so far this year, including 496 in England.
The BBC has reported on cases found in Scotland and the South West, and the NFU has made clear its concerns for the South East.
Livestock board chair for the East of England Hugh Broom said: "If your animals are not vaccinated already, please speak to your vet about getting on the list...it could just take a westerly wind to send the disease our way."
Bluetongue virus (BTV) is an insect-borne viral disease affecting sheep and cattle among other animals.
It is spread by biting midges and does not affect humans or human food safety.
According to the NFU, it is often fatal in sheep and can cause abortions in cows, temporary infertility in bulls and deformities in newborn calves.
Broom, who farms near Dorking, Surrey, and also represents livestock farmers in Kent and Sussex, said the vaccination was "safe, affordable and quick".
The farmer said he understood that many things, including the lack of rainfall and rising fertiliser prices, were out of farmers' control at the moment.
"Vaccinating your animals is completely in your control," he added.
The NFU said that, in order to reduce the risk of bluetongue, farmers were moving high-risk or non-vaccinated stock away from wet, low-lying, or sheltered areas.
They are also keeping vulnerable animals housed during dawn and dusk when midge activity peaks.
Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Surrey on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: The National Farmers' Union is urging farmers in the South East to vaccinate their livestock against bluetongue as soon as possible. Government figures show 517 cases of the virus have been reported in the UK this year. The insect-borne disease affects sheep and cattle and can be fatal.
key_points: There are over 500 reported cases of bluetongue in the UK this year.
The NFU urges South East farmers to vaccinate their animals against the virus.
Bluetongue is spread by biting midges and affects sheep and cattle.
Farmers are also moving vulnerable stock away from wet areas and keeping them housed during peak midge activity.

title: ‘My ability to cope was unravelling’: how I navigated ADHD and childbirth – and seven things I learned
author: Sarah Marsh
content:
It’s 7am in a postnatal ward. I’ve been brought here having given birth around four hours earlier. I’m hot and have not slept since arriving at the hospital at 9pm for an induction, only to go into labour spontaneously before it could begin. All around me is incandescent hospital light and the sound of crying newborns. This would be challenging enough for someone who isn’t neurodivergent, but coupled with my attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) I could feel my ability to cope unravelling.
I remember looking around, crying, unable to shut off the noise in my brain. “What if I don’t ever sleep again,” the little voice asked. I shut my eyes and the noise grew. Then there was my newborn son, lying next to me in a cot, and the fact that I had absolutely no idea how to look after him. I pressed the emergency buzzer and told the midwife who arrived that I could not breathe and needed to be discharged immediately. She said they couldn’t do that because I was under the mental health team and needed to speak to them first. I cried more.
The rest of my stay in hospital is a blur. I begged anyone who came near my bed for sleeping pills. Eventually, with the help of my midwife and the mental health team, I was sent home that day.
It was only a year later, when I learned I was neurodivergent, that my struggles that day finally made sense. Certain parts of becoming a parent are simply harder with ADHD. Birth itself strips away any sense of predictability, and ADHD brains often manage anxiety by controlling their environment – being on a postnatal ward, with its constant lights, noises, and the feeling of being trapped inside, can be sensory overload.
![A woman sitting in a wooden playhouse with two children](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3ed25d23998e82f231fd26006e0e4ec308429f13/0_0_10000_7500/master/10000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The NHS currently has no consistent, ADHD-specific maternity pathway, so support for women with ADHD during childbirth varies widely and often depends on individual clinicians recognising and accommodating their needs, rather than on a standardised system.
When I gave birth, I was told afterwards that nothing really exists to support women and research is limited. It prompted me to write a book about ADHD and becoming a parent to help other women. Here’s a summary of what I learned.
Hormones affect those with ADHD more
Scientists believe that ADHD symptoms can be affected by hormones, and a study by King’s College London is aiming to look at exactly that. Oestrogen and progesterone are the two main female hormones, and both rise rapidly in pregnancy. Oestrogen has a stimulating effect on the brain – it boosts dopamine and serotonin, the chemicals behind focus, mood, and motivation – so when it’s high, ADHD symptoms tend to ease. Progesterone, which rises after ovulation and in pregnancy, may have an opposing effect on dopamine signalling to oestrogen and can even make ADHD medication less effective.
In the first trimester, both hormones rise fast. Things often improve in the second trimester, when oestrogen levels are higher and more stable. Anecdotally, I heard from psychiatrists I interviewed that some women find their ADHD symptoms ease in pregnancy as a result. For others, this isn’t the case. There’s no universal rule, as hormones are complicated.
A large study found that women with ADHD were over five times more likely to be diagnosed with postpartum depression than women without ADHD, because hormone levels drop suddenly after birth. In terms of coping, simply being aware of these changes is valuable – it lets you protect yourself during the periods when your endocrine system is affected most. Staying active can help as it releases endorphins and is a natural mood booster, as can putting together a postnatal plan in advance, to relieve pressure and make sure you have as much support as you need after birth.
Medication
For those with ADHD, the more pressing concern might be whether they can continue taking medication.
When I was pregnant with my son, I continued taking the antidepressant citalopram. My psychiatrist explained that the potential risks associated with the drug were relatively small, and that the evidence linking it to harm was inconclusive. I weighed things up and decided that, for me, the risks of stopping a medication I’d been taking for seven years were greater than the potential risks of continuing it.
As for ADHD medication, there isn’t a tremendous amount of research on its use during pregnancy, mainly due to the ethical challenges of studying pregnant women. Dr Catherine Durkin, joint presidential lead for women and mental health at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, says the key is to balance risk. “What are we treating? What are the risks of not treating it?” she says. Durkin also says that data on ADHD medication and breastfeeding is limited, and recommends discussing the matter with your specialist.
Know your rights
![A pregnant woman is seated while conversing with a medical professional during a checkup.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/531067a0792c24bb1371587fdb5ed9b7fd4f9ef1/0_0_7705_5137/master/7705.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
If you have ADHD, you have more power and agency in the healthcare system than you might think. Not every healthcare professional understands ADHD, so it’s vital to know where to access appropriate perinatal mental health support if you need it. People with ADHD may be more vulnerable to experiencing mental health difficulties during pregnancy and the postnatal period, making appropriate support particularly important. Victoria White, a doula who specialises in helping those who are neurodivergent, says that under the Equality Act 2010, anyone with a chronic illness or disability can request reasonable adjustments to their care. “Neurodivergence falls under that,” she says. “Technically, self-diagnosis should count too, though that can be more difficult.”
A reasonable adjustment could be as simple as visiting the birthing suite in advance to reduce anxiety. Laura Spence, a midwife who trained in Scotland 14 years ago, says: “Women have the right to most things; it’s their birth, their body, their baby. Nothing is set in stone.”
Create a birth plan
My son was measuring small, and my obstetrician wanted him to be born by 39 weeks because they were concerned he might not be growing as well as he should. His estimated size had dropped from the 14th to the 10th percentile – in other words, he was now smaller than approximately 90% of babies at the same stage of pregnancy. To help encourage labour to start, I was given a membrane sweep, a procedure where a midwife or doctor gently separates the membranes surrounding the baby from the cervix.
Three days later my waters broke and I was told I had 24 hours for labour to start before they would need to induce me due to the increased risk of infection that comes with the waters being broken for too long. Luckily, moments before my booked induction, contractions started. Labour progressed quickly and was around five hours in total.
If you have ADHD, do what you need to get through birth. Neurodivergent individuals may require more control, knowing when and how things will unfold. Or less. Ask for what you need.
Plan for the postnatal period
![A pregnant woman holding her stomach and taking notes on a notepad](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/59d3bf8146c9bbdb49aafcf35bb8ff2117a21fd0/0_0_6720_4480/master/6720.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the car on the way home from the hospital, I kept looking over at my son, worrying about every bump in the road and whether his tiny body could withstand it. My partner and I had no plan for what life would look like now. We hadn’t thought about a sleep schedule and barely had all the essentials such as a cot and a pram. In hindsight, a plan would have been smart. If I could go back, I’d focus on five key areas: sleep, feeding, changing clothes and nappies, stimulation, and love. That’s all your baby needs early on. I would have made a plan about how to manage each of these.
It’s also helpful to note down essential appointments in advance: vaccinations, health checks and registering with a GP. Delegate this type of admin to your partner or a family member. You’ll be recovering. If you need mental health support, arrange it in advance.
Ignore unhelpful expectations
The idea of the perfect mother is a myth, but those with ADHD may feel the sting of falling short more acutely. After all, if you have ADHD, you’ve likely been criticised your whole life for doing things “wrong”. Focus on your strengths, whatever they may be. Having ADHD has made me resilient and I am much more able to cope than I give myself credit for.
Watch out for burnout
Returning to work after having a child can sometimes mean the end of the workday simply marks the start of another shift – managing the household, bedtime routines and family needs. It can be hard to balance work, family and a social life. This challenge is amplified for those with ADHD, who tend to overcommit and then burn out. Watch for the key signs of burnout – exhaustion and fatigue, sadness and depression, a lack of motivation, and general disconnection from others – and prioritise your self-care. If you start to feel as if you might be about to hit a wall, then make more time for yourself.
summary: Navigating childbirth and the postnatal period with ADHD can present intense sensory and emotional challenges due to unpredictability and hormonal shifts. The NHS currently lacks a consistent, ADHD-specific maternity pathway, meaning support often varies. However, understanding how hormones affect ADHD, knowing your legal rights to reasonable adjustments, and planning ahead for birth and the postnatal period can help manage these difficulties.
key_points: Hormones fluctuations during and after pregnancy significantly impact ADHD symptoms, with a sudden drop in hormones after birth increasing the risk of postpartum depression.
Under the Equality Act 2010, individuals with neurodivergence can request reasonable adjustments to their maternity care, such as visiting the birthing suite in advance.
Research on ADHD medication use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited, requiring patients to carefully weigh risks and benefits with a specialist.
Creating a detailed postnatal plan and delegating essential admin tasks to partners can help reduce overwhelm and prevent burnout.

title: What is salmonella, how does it spread and are eggs safe to eat?
author: Denis Campbell
content:
Contaminated eggs have infected 207 people with salmonella across the UK, killing one and hospitalising 34.
Eggs imported into Britain and eaten in cafes and restaurants were the source, the UK Health Security Agency has said. The outbreak has prompted public concern. But what is salmonella, and are eggs safe to eat?
What is salmonella?
“Salmonella isn’t a single ‘bug’ but the name we give to a whole group of bacteria that can cause infection in humans. There are over 2,500 different types of salmonella bacteria,” said Dr Malick Gibani, a clinical associate professor at Imperial College London.
Most disease in the UK is caused by just a few of those 2,500 types. They are usually found in contaminated animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. But chocolate, peanut butter and cucumbers have also been at the centre of previous UK outbreaks.
Salmonella can be spread by contaminated drinking water, contact with animals, person-to-person spread or poor food hygiene and preparation, “particularly when cooked food comes into contact with contaminated and undercooked or raw foods”, said Gibani. Storing food poorly, which allows the bacteria to replicate, and not cooking contaminated foods thoroughly are also risks.
How does salmonella affect people?
Salmonella causes an infection of the gut – gastroenteritis – and that leads to food poisoning. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and a fever, though some people also feel very tired and suffer sore muscles and joints. Symptoms can appear within a few hours to a few days.
Gibani said: “Salmonella can be unpleasant for a few days. In most cases, people will get better without any treatment, but in some instances antibiotics might be needed, particularly in vulnerable groups. Antibiotics are usually only needed when there’s a severe bloodstream infection, but thankfully this is pretty rare in healthy adults in the UK.”
Who is most at risk?
Children and older adults, people whose immune systems are suppressed, perhaps because they are taking chemotherapy drugs for cancer, and those with underlying health conditions can be more severely affected.
Scientists aren’t sure why. But, Gibani said, the fact that such groups are hit more severely shows that “there’s definitely an immune component which influences severity”.
“In some people, instead of just causing an infection inside the gut, salmonella bacteria can spread into the blood, which can be very dangerous. When this happens it can cause a severe sepsis-like illness,” he said.
“We often consider salmonella as a disease with an ‘image problem’. It can be dismissed as ‘just food poisoning’ and a bit of diarrhoea. But severe and invasive cases kill thousands of people a year around the world.”
Severe infection is a big problem in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, which has high rates of salmonella bloodstream infections, including in children who have recently had malaria, are malnourished or have advanced or untreated HIV.
Should you avoid eggs?
No. But you should choose the eggs you buy carefully, experts say.
Kimberly Coffin, the technical director of supply chain assurance at LRQA, a global risk management firm based in Birmingham, said: “The safest choice for consumers is to buy eggs produced in the UK which carry the red lion mark. These eggs come from hens that have been vaccinated against salmonella.”
She offered other tips to avoid catching salmonella. “Cooking eggs and egg-containing dishes until both yolk and white are firm, or to a temperature of 71C, is the best way to provide consumer safety from salmonella.
“It’s also important not to use any cracked or broken eggs, nor eggs that have external evidence of wet or dry residues due to the potential for ingress of potential microbiological contaminates on the surface into the egg. Washing dirty eggs before use does not reduce this risk and, in fact, increases the risk.”
Should the public be alarmed?
Gibani said: “It’s understandable that people might be worried about salmonella and what and where they ‘should’ eat. The public should be aware and informed but not alarmed.”
He and Coffin both stressed that the UK has robust systems of protection against salmonella, brought in after previous outbreaks, such as the vaccination programme and strong food standards and controls, especially for eggs. But no regime is failsafe, as this new outbreak shows.
The UKHSA website is a useful source of information about salmonella.
summary: Contaminated imported eggs have infected 207 people with salmonella across the UK, resulting in one death and 34 hospitalizations. Salmonella is a group of bacteria causing gut infections and food poisoning, spreading mainly through contaminated animal products, poor food hygiene, and water. While most people recover without treatment, vulnerable groups face higher risks of severe, invasive illness. Experts advise consumers not to avoid eggs entirely, but instead to buy UK eggs with the red lion mark, cook them thoroughly until firm, and avoid cracked or washed eggs.
key_points: A salmonella outbreak linked to imported eggs has caused 207 infections, 34 hospitalizations, and one death in the UK.
Symptoms of salmonella infection include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting, and a fever.
Children, older adults, and those with suppressed immune systems are at the highest risk for severe illness.
Experts recommend buying UK eggs with the red lion mark and cooking them until both the yolk and white are firm to prevent infection.
Washing dirty eggs does not reduce risk and actually increases the likelihood of bacterial contamination.

title: Denying that ADHD is real is a harmful mistake
author: Chris Abbott; Miranda Levy
content:
![Dr Chris Abbott, Chief Medical Officer of Care ADHD](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/14/TELEMMGLPICT000498224433_17867249841390_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqF4gK46GOnJavFqlzWmmLlh2b7M0ItnRL6jFWzM60U5I.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Dr Chris Abbott, Chief Medical Officer of Care ADHD](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/14/TELEMMGLPICT000498224433_17867249841390_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqF4gK46GOnJavFqlzWmmLlh2b7M0ItnRL6jFWzM60U5I.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Channel 4’s new documentary The Great ADHD Myth? heard medical experts question whether ADHD is a genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or a social construct. Dr Iona Heath, the former president of the Royal College of General Practitioners, was among them, who said in an interview with The Telegraph that she “would ban the label ADHD”. Now, we hear from the Chief Medical Officer at the Centre for ADHD Research and Excellence about his perspective having watched the documentary.
ADHD is not just about forgetting your car keys or losing your phone. It’s unlikely you have the condition if your concentration wavers on repetitive tasks, or you occasionally drift into daydreams. For those who have ADHD, their lives have been a constant struggle since childhood, and denying that ADHD is “real” can cause significant harm to children, adults and families. A diagnosis can be life-changing.
Which is why, as chief medical officer at the Centre for ADHD Research and Excellence (Care ADHD), news of a Channel 4 documentary, The Great ADHD Myth?, makes me angry. It’s a sloppy title that negates the difficulties and challenges people with ADHD go through before getting a diagnosis or receiving effective care.
Watching the documentary made me frustrated. The title – with the question mark – made you feel there was going to be a debate. Where was the debate? I found it completely one-sided and the language was inflammatory.
The show ignored years of evidence, science and research. They completely ignored discussion of the non-medical treatments of ADHD. It was binary and over-simplified. They appear to have spoken to a carefully curated set of individuals, none of whom as far as I am aware are qualified as experts in ADHD.
I doubt the programme-makers thought through what this TV show might mean to someone who has finally received an ADHD diagnosis, only for their family and friends to watch a show casting doubts on whether the condition even exists. Patients had finally started to push back on the stigma, only to have all that whipped out from under them again. But for those living with ADHD, the impact of the condition on their lives is all too real.
![Max Pemberton in The Great ADHD Myth?](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/14/TELEMMGLPICT000497644186_17867250398200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Everyone needs to understand that there’s a difference between a child who is a bit energetic or forgetful, and a child who can’t stop moving and in one school term loses five different PE kits, three winter coats and has no idea where his pen or textbooks went. It’s not one pen. It’s not one gym kit: for a child with ADHD, everything gets lost.
Two years ago, I saw a 16-year-old boy who had left education, and was in and out of trouble with the police. He had been labelled as having a conduct disorder. But within a year of effective medication and therapy, he was able to take on an apprenticeship as a mechanic. It opened up the possibility he would one day own a car, get a mortgage, start a family. Without this intervention, there is a high chance he might be in prison right now.
Then there was the student nurse, in her final year, who was falling behind with her studies because she was unable to focus. She was so worried that she’d miss or forget something on her course that her day was full of alarms, notes and yellow sticky reminders. This young woman had been diagnosed with anxiety, but that was just a symptom of her ADHD. After the appropriate treatment, she now works for a hospital in the Midlands. Life is about choices. ADHD can rob you of them.
There’s been a lot of criticism of ADHD lately. But ADHD is absolutely not a social construct, as some have termed it. It is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms in three key areas: hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention. These are always present and severe enough to impact your entire life, whether at home, school, or work. We can all be distracted sometimes or make impulsive decisions. That doesn’t mean we have ADHD.
Crucially, all these symptoms have to have been present from birth. You don’t suddenly develop ADHD. The 16-year-old prospective mechanic had been unable to concentrate as far back as story time at nursery, the student nurse had spent her school days gazing out of the window. If a 35-year-old has diagnosed themselves via social media, there might be something else going on, such as anxiety, but it’s not necessarily ADHD. We need to ensure the diagnosis is right.
Much has been written – often negatively – about the rise in ADHD diagnoses, but ADHD is not a new or “trendy” condition, and those living with it do not deserve to have to deal with this backlash. It has been 200 years since a Scottish doctor first observed a difficulty sustaining attention in certain young children, a condition renamed the “hyperkinetic reaction of childhood” in the 1960s.
And while it’s true there has been an increase in the numbers being diagnosed, this does not mean that people are being over-diagnosed. Commentators often confuse the two. NHS England estimates that 5 per cent of the population – around 2.5 million people – have ADHD, but only 1.19 per cent – or 700,000 – have received a diagnosis. The idea that we are over-diagnosing is absolutely untrue.
![Dr Chris Abbott, Chief Medical Officer of Care ADHD](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/14/TELEMMGLPICT000498224425_17867249960920_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
What has increased is an awareness of the condition. This is actually very helpful, not just for individuals, but for the schools these pupils attend. When I was at school back in the 1990s, teachers would tell students: “You’re naughty. Sit down, stop getting distracted, and focus.” But they never wondered whether this child was struggling, or asked what they could do to help.
Some people complain that an ADHD diagnosis conveys an unfair advantage. For example, for the employee who gets extra time at work, or the child who gets to jump the queue at a theme park – as is mentioned in the Channel 4 documentary. But ADHD diagnosis does not automatically grant you access to anything.
I hate the term “disability”, but people sometimes need help, whether that be extra time in an exam, or visual aids at work, such as a paper calendar or pictures instead of printed instructions. That young child at the theme park might also have a diagnosis of autism or a learning disability and not understand the need to queue. Letting them go to the front might make the day more enjoyable for them, and the people around them.
A main worry for me is people self-diagnosing on TikTok or Instagram, which belittles the struggles that many genuinely face. If you feel you might have an issue, it’s important to find doctors, nurses, or clinical psychologists who understand that and have regular group discussions with their colleagues to confirm a diagnosis. Ask whether they are registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), whether they have NHS contracts or are following NICE guidelines. If they do, they’re going to be using gold-standard diagnostic tools and only hiring qualified practitioners. The treatment has to be evidence-based.
Where medication comes into the equation, clinicians need to follow guidelines. My clinic, for example, gave a 10-week pause after diagnosis and before prescribing, so the patient can carefully weigh up their decision to take medication. For an adult, therapy also might help. A person who gets an ADHD diagnosis might think: “All my life, I believed I was stupid.” That can be overwhelming, leaving their self-esteem at rock bottom.
Listening to patients is vital: hearing from people whose lives have been significantly affected by the condition and then improved by positive diagnosis. Many are put off or anxious that they – or their children – are going to end up being medicated. But from my own observations, fewer than 50 per cent of younger children are given medication, and around seven in 10 adults. These treatments can have significant results, but we are increasingly moving towards a more holistic approach, with coaching and therapy.
Most of all, people need to realise that an ADHD diagnosis isn’t just about forgetting your wallet or being a bit more fidgety than the average person. Labelling yourself after watching an Instagram video will never be helpful. It’s time to move away from alarmist talk of “myths” and misdiagnosis and have a sensible conversation about helping those dealing with a condition that can ruin lives.
A Channel 4 spokesman said: “This documentary does not deny the lived experience of those diagnosed with ADHD, but does present the views of an extensive range of senior medical experts – many of whom work or have worked with the NHS or have held presidential roles at professional membership bodies – who seek to question the conventional understanding of ADHD and if it is a neurodevelopmental condition. They also ask whether modern living has contributed to a rise in diagnoses, and whether there may be better alternatives for some children than medication.”
As told to Miranda Levy
Dr Chris Abbott is an NHS-trained consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist. He is chief medical officer at Care ADHD, where he provides clinical leadership on ADHD assessments, diagnoses, and services in the UK
summary: Dr Chris Abbott, chief medical officer at Care ADHD, argues that dismissing ADHD as a social construct or a myth is harmful to children, adults, and families who struggle with the condition. He criticizes Channel 4's documentary, The Great ADHD Myth?, for ignoring scientific evidence and worsening the stigma faced by patients. Abbott notes that proper diagnosis and holistic treatment, including medication and therapy, can be life-changing and emphasizes that the UK is facing a rise in awareness rather than an over-diagnosis of the condition.
key_points: Denying that ADHD is a real neurodevelopmental condition causes significant harm and invalidates the lifelong struggles of those affected.
Channel 4's documentary ignored years of science, research, and non-medical treatments while presenting a one-sided view.
NHS data shows that only 1.19 per cent of the population has received an ADHD diagnosis, despite an estimated 5 per cent having the condition, proving it is not being over-diagnosed.
Proper diagnosis and evidence-based treatments, such as medication and therapy, can drastically improve the lives of patients and open up new opportunities.
Self-diagnosing via social media platforms like TikTok or Instagram undermines the severe challenges faced by individuals with genuine ADHD.

title: Doctors raise alarm over H. pylori drug resistance
author: Salome Gregory
content:
Doctors raise alarm over H. pylori drug resistance
H. pylori, the bacterium, which can cause inflammation of the stomach lining and peptic ulcers is common in Tanzania but has increasingly become resistant to drugs. PHOTO | FILE
Dar es Salaam. For some patients, treating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is no longer a straightforward process, with doctors reporting cases in which commonly used medicines fail to clear the infection.
The bacterium, which can cause inflammation of the stomach lining, peptic ulcers and, in the long term, increase the risk of stomach cancer, is common in Tanzania and many other parts of the world.
Its symptoms, including stomach pain, bloating, heartburn and nausea, are increasingly being reported by patients seeking medical care.
Health experts, however, are concerned about possible antibiotic resistance, which can make standard treatment less effective and leave patients experiencing recurring symptoms.
For Jeremiah Isdory, the problem returned twice within six months despite treatment for peptic ulcers.
“I had been experiencing stomach pain for a very long time.. When I went to hospital, I was diagnosed with peptic ulcers and given treatment. After two months, the problem returned,” he said.
Another patient said he underwent treatment for H. pylori with month-long courses of medication more than twice before seeking care at another hospital. “I went to another hospital where I was given medication for two weeks. That helped and the bacteria was gone,” he said.
The experiences have highlighted the importance of testing, appropriate treatment and follow-up, particularly as doctors report encountering cases in which some medicines no longer work as expected.
Aga Khan Hospital gastroenterologist and hepatologist Dr Masolwa Ng’wanasai said H. pylori requires proper diagnosis and treatment and patients should not start medication before consulting a health professional.
“From our experience as health professionals, we have recently encountered a challenge of drug resistance in this bacterium. Some medicines that have been used for a long time are no longer treating the infection effectively,” he said.
Dr Ng’wanasai said some patients may need alternative medicines or referral to another facility where the required treatment is available. However, he noted that Tanzania does not yet have a national study establishing the extent of H. pylori drug resistance. “So far, we have not seen any study that has been conducted in the country on this challenge,” he said.
The Ministry of Health’s Director of Medical Services, Hamad Nyembea, said H. pylori is treated with antibiotics in accordance with national treatment guidelines. He said patients should undergo testing after completing treatment to determine whether the infection has been cleared.
“As with other diseases, after completing the course of treatment, a patient should be tested to confirm whether they have recovered. If the bacteria is still present, the patient should continue treatment according to the guidelines. Therefore, there are times when a patient may need to take additional medication,” Mr Nyembea said.
According to the treatment guidelines, initial H. pylori therapy includes a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), clarithromycin and amoxicillin. Where resistance develops, patients may need second-line treatment.
Dr Ngwegwe Damas warned against self-medication, particularly buying antibiotics from pharmacies without first undergoing medical assessment.
He said patients could end up taking the wrong medicine or dose, potentially contributing to antimicrobial resistance. “It is very important for people to follow proper hospital treatment instead of treating themselves or going to a pharmacy to obtain medicine without undergoing tests. This will help patients receive the right treatment depending on the severity of their condition,” he said.
Dr Damas also advised patients to undergo follow-up testing at the time recommended by their doctor rather than assuming that the infection has cleared because symptoms have disappeared. “It is very important to test again four weeks after treatment to confirm that the bacteria has been completely eliminated and to prevent the problem from recurring,” he said.
Consultant nephrologist at Benjamin Mkapa Hospital Dr Kessy Shija said inappropriate or prolonged use of some medicines could contribute to antimicrobial resistance.
“Sometimes certain medicines may have already led to resistance. When a patient keeps coming back, resistance can develop,” he said. Dr Shija said recurring symptoms should not automatically lead to patients being given the same medicines without further assessment.
He urged patients to provide doctors with a complete history of previous treatment, including medicines they had already taken and tests they had undergone. “A patient should say that they have previously been treated with these particular medicines or that they have undergone tests several times and received certain medication. This enables the doctor to determine the appropriate way to help them,” he said.
Experts also warned that frequently changing health facilities without providing previous treatment records can make it difficult for doctors to establish a patient’s medical history and determine the appropriate next step.
H. pylori can spread between people through contaminated food or water and poor hand hygiene. Experts say the risk may be higher in areas with inadequate sanitation and limited access to safe water.

summary: Doctors in Tanzania are raising concerns over increasing drug resistance in Helicobacter pylori, a common bacterium that causes stomach inflammation and peptic ulcers. Commonly used medicines are failing to clear the infection in some patients, leading to recurring symptoms. Health experts warn against self-medication and improper antibiotic use, emphasizing the importance of proper diagnosis, follow-up testing, and sharing complete medical histories.
key_points: H. pylori is a common bacterium in Tanzania that causes stomach inflammation, peptic ulcers, and increases the risk of stomach cancer.
Health professionals report a growing challenge of drug resistance, where long-used medicines no longer effectively treat the infection.
Experts warn against self-medication and buying antibiotics from pharmacies without proper medical assessment, which contributes to antimicrobial resistance.
Patients are advised to undergo follow-up testing four weeks after completing treatment to confirm the bacteria has been completely eliminated.
Providing a complete history of previous treatments to doctors helps prevent recurring symptoms and ensures appropriate alternative care is given.

title: “I Fantasized About Getting Hit By A Car”: 25 New Mothers Share The PPD Warning Signs They Ignored, But Don’t Want Other Moms To
author: Kanksha Raina
content:
Postpartum depression has been making the rounds in the news recently. As much as we know of postpartum depression, there's very little we actually know about it. Here's some added perspective on the issue: According to the CDC, roughly 1 in 8 new mothers report symptoms of postpartum depression, which is about 12.7% women—affecting upwards of 400,000 mothers a year. A CDC study also found that symptoms don't necessarily appear immediately after birth, but 9-10 months after it. Several women do not report these symptoms, because they are just that tricky and not often talked about in the context of childbirth. These statistics only emphasize what we've been talking about forever: we need to take women's pain seriously.
As I dug deeper into this, I went to Reddit in search of first-person stories to understand the severity of PPD. And I found these Reddit threads—they really put into perspective the enormity of childbirth and how it impacts new mamas. And here I am, sharing it with you to shed some light on it, so we all leave with a little less misinformation and a little more empathy.
Warning: This post contains discussions of self-harm, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts. Reader discretion is advised.
Responses have been edited for length and clarity.
Here are the stories of 25 moms who figured out that they did, in fact, have postpartum depression:
1. "I was so tired in the first few weeks that I started seeing things “run by” out of the corner of my eye all the time. I also convinced myself that there was something staring at me from one of the pictures in the nursery and I talked to it a couple of times. We came to an understanding that it could stay as long as we were on the same page about childcare and it would help me watch my baby…now I know that I was dangerously close to post partum psychosis."
2. "I remember waking up bolt upright terrified that I’d fallen asleep in the bed and the baby was tangled in the blankets somewhere. I never once had, but the cold sweats in those split seconds were something else... meanwhile baby's just chilling in his cot."
3. "My mom looked at me and said "Wow. You look horrible. Have you eaten?" And I realized I hadn't eaten in almost three days and had sunk in purple rings under my eyes. She was four months old and I just wasn't doing the basic things to survive."
4. "Anger. Angry at my cats, to the point where them just existing made me angry. Angry at my partner. Constantly snapping at him, bitter and mad that his life didn’t seem to just stop the way mine had. Angry at myself for “ruining my life”. It came to a head one day when I was trying to open a food package and completely lost it. I felt everything that day, anger, depression, suicidal, and I knew I needed help."
5. "I had fantasies about getting hit by a car so I would be laid up in a hospital and not have to deal with my family. I ignored that and then the fantasies changed and I kept thinking that if I died it wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world, I didn’t feel like I had much use to anyone anyway. When I said something along those lines in the form of a joke to my mom she made me call my doctor right away."
— Anonymous
6. "When every time bubs made a noise or even woke up I got so agitated and mad that I turned to my partner and said, "If you do not look after him right now I will hurt him." I knew that wasn't OK and got help the very next day. People were telling me I might have PPD and were checking on me all the time but I ignored them until I realized I had gone over the edge."
7. "I already had depression my entire pregnancy and I have a long history of it as well, so I knew something was wrong when I was irrationally angry all the time but unfortunately I didn’t take myself to the hospital when I realized this. I ended up having suicidal and homicidal thoughts towards myself and my baby, and the last day I had her before I went to the hospital I screamed at her. It makes me sad to type this because she is a great baby and I love her so much, so reliving those times were hard. But a week away at a hospital and getting professional help worked."
"If you think you have PPD get help now, you might not need to go to the hospital but you should seek professional help if you feel miserable and you’re questioning if you have it or not." — garden-in-the-girl
8. "I'm not sure I had depression but definitely some postpartum anxiety. I kept telling my husband I didn't feel like myself. I didn't enjoy anything. I was teaching at the time. I got frustrated at a student and screamed at him. That is unbelievably out of character for me. I honestly have no idea why I did it. I just found myself screaming before I could stop myself. (I apologized to him later). Then one night my toddler wanted me to read a book and kept pushing it on me. I took it and threw it across the room. Again, unbelievably out of character. Never in my life have I thrown something out of anger. Got myself on some anxiety meds and finally feel like myself again."
— sc0721
9. "My son was a year old. Everything made me angry. I cried on my way to work every day for four months. My husband avoided conversations with me because I was mean and short tempered. I didn't want to shower, or do anything. Asking for help was the best thing I ever did."
— venyse1
10. "Couldn't brush my teeth."
— Anonymous
12. "I was cutting garlic and suddenly I saw the pointy end of the blade I was using. I lifted it up to my wrist. I cut the surface of my skin a little, heard my little one's voice cry out. Her cry stopped me. I spent the next two hours talking to a crisis counsellor about suicide. This happened after I had been getting help with my GP and psychologist. But over the Christmas break I paused my treatments, and family stress piled on with my family and the JUST NO-in-laws. It’s been a few months now, I’m getting more regular time with my psychologist. Little one has gone to childcare and we have gone no-contact with the just no in-laws. My mental health has taken such a turn for the good. I still believe angels were watching over me that day when I tried to take my own life. My little one's cry saved me."
13. "One night I was staring at the baby monitor with tears running down my face as I looked up what hotel I was going to so that I could kill myself the next day. I didn't want my family burdened with my body when it was all over. I can't remember why I didn't go to be honest. A lot of that time is a big, black hole with a few patches of memory. He was smack in the middle of the four month sleep regression. We started sleep training and moved him to his own room, and finally things started to turn around. Anyone who is struggling, this is your wake up call. Talk to someone. I was so silent about my pain that my husband still doesn't know how close I came. No one in my life could have helped me because no one knew. It's NOT supposed to be that hard. You are NOT broken or wrong or less than. Talk to someone, anyone. Tomorrow is another day as long as you let it be."
14. "Hallucinations. So many hallucinations. My baby's face would morph into demonic ghostly creepy scary as fuck faces. I would look at the crib and the bars would start dancing, mocking me."
— Anonymous
15. "When I literally wanted to throw my daughter, because of her constant screaming. I hate admitting this."
"Had a colic baby and can confirm, even without PPD this is a legitimate feeling. My husband and I BOTH had some pretty intense conversations about how triggering our son’s crying was." — bennynthejetsss
16. "I think it's different for everyone symptom-wise, but the main thing is knowing something is not right and that you feel like you need help, regardless of how minute or inconsequential. For a more specific example, I felt like a failure as a mother, and a wife. I felt like nothing I did was very good enough and that my kids were better off without me.
