I could barely keep up with housework or handle my little one starting to explore the environment. I would get overwhelmed very easily. I would get so frustrated with myself that I would get angry very easily. I would cry a lot, feel sad, overwhelmed, angry, and numb. Sleep was sporadic at best (which did not help). I sought therapy after a night of no sleep and my little one was up in the middle of the night again crying and was inconsolable. I remember my husband trying to soothe baby but was still crying for mama. I ran back into the room screaming, "Put the baby up for adoption, I can't do this anymore."
"The look on my husband's face said it all. I felt devastated and awful. My baby at that time was a year old. I didn't realize you could get postpartum that long after. But I was also trying to wean baby off breast, and unbeknownst to us pregnant, then shortly after miscarried so my hormones were a hot mess." — RozaHathaway
17. "I had pretty much stopped sleeping unless my twins were no more than a couple feet away from me (and even then I was waking up frequently to check on them), because I was convinced somewhere along the way that there was a woman living in our walls/attic who was going to sneak into the room at night and take one or both of them while we slept. It started off as a small fear from a weird nightmare or a movie or some combination of things I've seen, but I was severely exacerbated one night when the boys went to sleep in their room and my husband and I slept in our room. When they finally woke up around midnight, I immediately looked at the monitor and saw these shadow hands grabbing one of the babies and pulling him out of view of the camera. I freaked out but didn't tell my husband what I saw, instead we just ran in there and picked up both boys and brought them into our room."
19. "I thought it was all just normal mom stuff until my world started falling apart and I spiraled into burnout. We had to move in with my in-laws while selling our house, my stress levels increased, I was snapping at everyone especially if the little one was crying. I thought I needed to reach out for help but didn’t say anything and then I got a call from my best friend’s mother. I hadn’t heard from my best friend since about 7:15 the night before. She died of a pulmonary embolism about 20 minutes after our last text. That was five months ago. In working through the grief with a therapist. I’ve pieced together that by the time my best friend died, I had been living with PPD for 8.5 months. I can identify when it started now, but it really spiraled before I did something about it."
— Anonymous
summary: According to the CDC, postpartum depression affects roughly 1 in 8 new mothers, with symptoms sometimes appearing months after birth. First-person accounts from Reddit highlight how many mothers ignored severe warning signs, including hallucinations, extreme anger, intrusive thoughts, and suicidal ideation. These personal stories emphasize the critical importance of recognizing these symptoms and seeking professional help.
key_points: Postpartum depression and related symptoms can appear months after childbirth and are frequently underreported.
Many new mothers experience severe warning signs such as overwhelming anger, sleep deprivation, and uncharacteristic outbursts.
Several mothers reported experiencing frightening hallucinations, extreme anxiety, and postpartum psychosis.
Extreme cases included intrusive thoughts of self-harm, suicidal ideation, and near-suicide attempts.
Seeking professional help, therapy, or medication proved essential for recovery for the mothers who shared their stories.

title: Children ‘must not eat runny eggs’ amid salmonella outbreak
author: Samuel Montgomery
content:
Parents should avoid feeding runny eggs to children under the age of five during the salmonella outbreak, health officials have said.
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has warned that under-5s, over-65s, pregnant women and those with weakened immune systems should avoid products that might contain uncooked or runny eggs.
Earlier this week, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) declared a national outbreak of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds fell ill.
Ian Young, the chief scientific adviser at the FSA, said: “If people are eating out or consuming eggs or egg-containing products from cafes and restaurants, then for those people in particular who are young, elderly, pregnant or vulnerable, it’s important to make sure that any eggs or egg products that you consume in those settings have been very well cooked.”
He added: “People need to be careful.”
summary: Health officials have warned that children under five and other vulnerable groups should avoid eating runny or uncooked eggs during a national salmonella outbreak. The Food Standards Agency issued the guidance after the UK Health Security Agency reported hundreds of illnesses and one death. Officials advise that eggs consumed outside the home by vulnerable populations must be thoroughly cooked.
key_points: A national salmonella outbreak has caused one death and hundreds of illnesses in the UK.
The Food Standards Agency advises children under five, pregnant women, over-65s, and vulnerable individuals to avoid runny eggs.
Vulnerable groups eating out should ensure all eggs and egg-containing products are thoroughly cooked.
The warning was issued by Ian Young, the chief scientific adviser at the FSA.

title: We found love while waiting for a kidney transplant
author: Susanna Galton
content:
![Lee Farrington and Kacey Brown on their wedding day](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676622_17857491304170_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_dJW5aFvbcu1sOWS1a52E6IcY_HIgcuv0hr90pgePGI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Lee Farrington and Kacey Brown on their wedding day](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676622_17857491304170_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_dJW5aFvbcu1sOWS1a52E6IcY_HIgcuv0hr90pgePGI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
With its chorus of beeping monitors and harsh fluorescent lights, the dialysis ward at Addenbrooke’s Hospital is an unlikely place for a love story.
For four hours at a time, three days a week, patients sit connected to machines that clean their blood while they wait for a kidney transplant. It is a place more associated with endurance than romance.
Yet it was here, between the whirr of dialysis machines and countless cups of tea, that Lee Farrington and Kacey Brown found something neither expected: the chance to fall in love.
An unexpected introduction
When Lee’s kidneys failed suddenly in 2022 after years of living with type 1 diabetes, his world changed overnight. The former flat roofer had to give up the work he had done since leaving school and begin dialysis while waiting for a kidney transplant. The average wait for a kidney from a deceased donor in the UK is two to three years.
“It was a frightening time,” he says. “I didn’t really know life without work.”
The dialysis unit paired him with an experienced patient who could help him adjust. “Meeting a new partner was the last thing on my mind,” says Lee, 49, who had recently separated and was starting dialysis for the first time. “I was told I was meeting a 40-year-old male bricklayer who could share some advice about how it all worked. But instead Kacey walked through the door.”
![Kacey and Lee taking a selfie together](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676491_17857491156195_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqYVJfVX8lOXOA23ylB4y8VcwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
At 45, Kacey, who worked as a visiting support officer for South Cambridge district council, had lived with kidney disease since she was 13. She received her first kidney transplant from her mother, Stephanie, at 15 and a second from an anonymous donor 15 years later. However, kidney transplants don’t last forever and she eventually returned to dialysis. As a patient representative, she had become the reassuring face for newcomers.
“Lee looked quite shy and rather terrified,” she says. “After his first session I was glad when he got moved to our side of the ward because then I could answer his questions and help him feel a bit more at ease.”
Four hours at a time
Initially, Lee’s questions were practical: why were the needles so large, what did the alarms mean, and was every unexpected sound a cause for panic?
“If you don’t have someone next to you like Kacey,” he says, “it’s overwhelming.” As the weeks passed, practical questions gave way to conversations about everything else. Both loved dogs and hiking, both came from close families, and both knew the pain of failed marriages.
![Lee Farrington wearing a mask in hospital as he sat through dialysis](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676619_17857491153503_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqthD_Iqv8BRmIZIzYBGWvrswZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Most patients watched television during dialysis. Lee and Kacey talked instead. “We could literally spend eight hours just chatting,” says Kacey. “I’d never had that before.” For almost a year they believed they had simply become close friends.
Looking back, everyone else had worked it out before they had. “The nurses had picked up on it, as had our families,” says Lee. “When we told them we were together, none of them were surprised.”
When friendship became something more
The turning point came in May 2023 when Lee suffered a heart attack during dialysis. “I didn’t even realise I was having a heart attack,” he says. “One of the nurses picked it up.” Watching him being wheeled away affected Kacey more deeply than she expected.
“I was so upset,” she says. “I’d seen patients become seriously unwell before, but I’d never been so emotionally affected. That’s when I realised I’d had feelings for him.”
Once Lee recovered, he asked her for coffee. Neither admitted they secretly regarded it as a first date.
Kacey remembers pulling over before collecting him from his parents’ house. “I had to have a chat with myself,” she laughs. “I kept thinking, ‘What are you doing? You know this guy inside out.’ But suddenly I had butterflies like a teenager.”
She chose jeans and a blue cardigan she hoped looked “nice but casual”. Meanwhile, Lee quietly bought himself a new blue shirt. Coffee turned into lunch at Nando’s. Over chicken and salad flowed six hours of conversation. “Time just becomes irrelevant when we’re together,” says Kacey.
![Lee Farrington and wife Kacey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676485_17857491155048_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq8EgjId6SjmMLVLSLMkcQiMwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Still, neither admitted how they felt. The following evening, during a phone call that stretched until four in the morning, Kacey finally broke the silence. “I felt a rush of adrenaline as the words left my mouth: ‘I’ve got a bit of a crush on you,’” she recalls.
She expected him to laugh or confess to a crush of his own. Instead, he took it further. “I just decided to go for it,” says Lee. “I told Kacey, ‘I love you. I’m in love with you.’”
“I was so shocked I just blurted, entirely truthfully, ‘I love you too,’” Kacey laughs. “The next morning Lee texted me saying he was walking on cloud nine. Both of us are in our 40s but we felt like adolescents.”
One moment still stands out for Lee.“The first time one of my daughters met Kacey, she just said, ‘Thank you for making my dad happy.’”
A proposal in hospital
Life continued to test them. Lee later suffered a second, more serious heart attack, requiring triple bypass surgery and temporarily removing him from the kidney transplant waiting list. For Kacey, balancing work, her own dialysis and caring for Lee was emotionally exhausting.
“When I got the call to say Lee had had a heart attack, I still had to have my dialysis session,” she says. “It’s not something you can put off.”
![Kacey sitting next to a dialysis treatment machine in hospital wearing a mask and blankets](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676494_17857491159194_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf-0Jyi0jPPD6Zx1hiwTPhlc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Yet both believe facing those challenges together strengthened their relationship.
“It’s been so important to have someone who understands exactly what you’re going through,” says Lee. “We both know the impact of kidney disease and can support each other through the rigours of treatment.”
“We eat the same diet and we’re both limited to about 500ml of fluid a day,” Kacey adds. “And if one of us says we’re too tired for sex, the other doesn’t take it personally,” she laughs. “We just get each other in a way neither of us has experienced before.”
Last November, during another hospital admission, Lee reached into his pocket for an engagement ring he had been carrying for weeks. “When I turned round, he was there on one knee with the ring,” says Kacey. “Of course I said yes. It was spontaneous, sincere and very romantic.”
“A hospital ward might seem an unusual place for a proposal,” says Lee, “but to us it felt exactly right.” The nurses applauded.
Looking beyond dialysis
The couple married in April this year surrounded by close family and friends. The following morning, they were back in the dialysis unit.
“Waiting for a transplant meant a honeymoon wasn’t possible,” says Kacey. “But our health has given us a unique perspective on life. We know there’s no time to waste.”
![Lee and Kacey on their wedding day](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/03/TELEMMGLPICT000494676489_17857491156916_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5yQLQqeH37t50SCyM4-zeBU--41c5Cba04Sh5SZbNZ8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Instead, they dream about the ordinary: travelling without planning around treatment, hiking with their three dogs and saying yes to spontaneous weekends away. “And I’d love to enjoy a pint and a massive banana split without worrying about my potassium levels,” grins Lee.
For now, though, they are simply grateful they found one another. “I never imagined I’d meet my future wife on dialysis and something so positive could come from it,” he says.
For two people who met while waiting for a kidney transplant, it turned out the greatest gift they found wasn’t a donor organ, but each other.
Kacey and Lee are raising awareness for Kidney Research UK. The charity offers support for all areas of kidney health, from a free online health check to find out if you’re at risk of kidney disease, to access to an online forum, recipes, exercise plans, tips and guidance.
summary: Lee Farrington and Kacey Brown met at Addenbrooke’s Hospital dialysis ward after Lee's kidneys failed in 2022 and Kacey volunteered as a patient representative to help newcomers. Bonded by shared experiences, medical challenges, and long conversations during treatments, their friendship eventually blossomed into romance. Lee proposed in a hospital ward, and the couple married in April before returning to dialysis the next morning.
key_points: Lee Farrington and Kacey Brown met in 2022 at a hospital dialysis ward where both were undergoing treatment for kidney disease.
After becoming close friends and supporting each other through medical emergencies like heart attacks, their relationship turned romantic in May 2023.
Lee proposed to Kacey during a hospital admission, and the couple got married in April.
Despite being unable to take a honeymoon due to their ongoing dialysis schedules, they continue to support each other and raise awareness for Kidney Research UK.

title: ‘If you’re just interested in answers, you are missing out’: philosopher Lani Watson on the power of asking questions
author: Zoe Williams
content:
Asking a question can change your mood, and having a questioning mindset can change your life – or, as the philosopher Lani Watson, an honorary fellow at the University of Edinburgh, is more likely to put it, “create change in your life”. When you live in an answer-oriented world, your phrasing tends towards the glib certainty, which is one of the things Watson – speaking to me from her home in Edinburgh – seems quite naturally to avoid.
Questioning fosters exploration and curiosity, she says. It changes your relationship to yourself and to others: it can make you fall in love; it can stop you going to war. Watson’s challenging book, Q: The Hidden Power of Questions in a World that Wants Answers, is written with a deceptive simplicity and an almost kindly encouragement, so you’re knee-deep into her proposition before you have even considered that it might turn out to be quite hard work.
The book is unusually interactive, asking the reader to read a sentence out loud, count the number of questions in a conversation between Watson and her wife, ask basic questions of themselves and stop to think about whether they can be answered. There’s an appendix at the end that promises to get you into a questioning frame of mind, which it turns out you have to write yourself (to be fair, there’s no trickery here; she does say that it’s empty – but in my reflexive quest for answers, I didn’t notice).
Here are some brass tacks, what you might coarsely call proof. From the world of neuroscience and evolutionary biology, we can see that asking questions stimulates dopamine, she explains, and “all that reward circuitry activates regardless of whether you get the answer, because the brain is trying to encourage you to continue exploring your environment”.
![Lani Watson raising her hands in the air](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4a5ec41229d15fb7c5d337661282a9db8bbb44a7/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Watson divides questioning into four stages. First is proto-questioning, common to all organisms, which is “exploratory information-seeking, tiny little nematodes seeking nutrition”. Then there’s private questioning, which connotes some intentionality, such as asking for information from your environment in a directed and deliberated way – in Watson’s example, you might see it in a penguin leaving its enclosure in Edinburgh zoo just because it’s figured out it can.
Then there’s social questioning, asking a question of another, which creates layers of joint attention and joint intentionality, and which, as far as we know, only humans do. “What’s over that horizon?” would be a classic example of social questioning sparking migration and changing human history. Finally, there is spoken questioning, which builds whole new layers of complexity and abstraction, since now we can jointly approach matters that aren’t right in front of us, that we may only have imagined.
If it sounds intuitive that questioning would be so pleasurable and generative, Watson’s book wonders, how did we end up in such an answer-oriented world? Education is measured in what we know, not what we ask. Our social norms guide us away from direct questioning, in case we look dumb, or intrusive. The overriding drive of our technological experimentation is towards directing all our questions to a machine and none to one another. And so-called “why-chaining” – repeatedly asking “why?” to whatever answer you get – is universally agreed to be the most annoying thing about a three-year-old.
There is a deep-seated desire for “cognitive closure”, Watson says, or, put more simply, knowing. Aporia, the state of bafflement or confusion, is uncomfortable, though some people tolerate it a lot better than others. Watson is an epistemologist by training, “so I’m invested in questions about knowledge. And I do regard myself to be a pretty extreme sceptic with respect to that tradition. I really don’t think we actually do come to know anything, truly, and I’m OK with that. It’s a really interesting conversation to have in a classroom with undergraduates; you have a huge range of levels of comfort with that conclusion, and its implications.”
I’m personally in the cognitive closure camp: I hate an ambiguous ending; I hate agreeing to differ. Someone’s four-year-old on social media the other day had a tantrum when he discovered infinity – he just wanted numbers to end – and I could hard-relate. But you can learn to live with aporia and be richer for it, Watson says. “It’s all about exposure – spending a lot of time confronting big unknowns. A theoretical physicist would be in a similar position.”
She grew up in Southampton, her father a geologist, her mother a researcher in social housing policy, and studied philosophy for her bachelor’s degree at the University of York, before becoming a research fellow at Oxford. “This questioning mindset that I look at is so fundamental to philosophical thinking that when I advocate for it, maybe I’m trying to introduce philosophy through a back door.”
![A man talking to a woman sitting at table in a garden](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2f1a8434c55bef7f62056af29fff514432c84cf7/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
While Watson’s academic discipline came to her so naturally, she’s not blind to its faults. “Philosophy has an identity crisis,” she says, “that’s been formed by 2,500 years of it being done by people who want to make it seem really difficult – abstract, complicated and not for you. When, in fact, it really is something we’re all doing all the time.” It’s sometimes called the “genius only” discipline, but it isn’t only that intimidating intellectual granite face that puts people off, Watson says; it’s also the idea of utility. “We have an aversion to abstraction that is ultimately driven, to some extent, by that problem of: what good is it to me? Why do I need to worry about that?”
Early in Watson’s consideration of what a question was, she stopped using question marks. This made her consider the history of this punctuation mark (it’s more recent than you would think: the court of Charlemagne), and its variations in other languages (there is one that just puts a circle above the salient word, which is cute), but she never went back to using question marks, and it never made any difference. “The only place where I feel an impulse to add a question mark is if I’m indicating that what looks like a statement is, in fact, a rhetorical question, which told me a lot about what the question mark was doing: it’s signalling something, rather than being a part of what a question is.”
But the other thing punctuation is good for, the reason you would have to prise it from my dead hands, is that it speeds up the eye, surely? “Yes, the lack of a question mark helps people to slow down, around this key moment of a question, which is exactly how you develop this questioning mindset.”
You’ll need that patience for the process Watson calls “assumption mining”, questioning yourself more deeply about what you think you already know. She describes this as a habitual intellectual exercise, almost deliberately casting yourself back into aporia. “I always think, when I do it myself, that when I get to space and time as my grounding assumptions, then I’ve reached the bottom. If we go beyond that, we’re back into theoretical physics.” Funny how we keep ending up there.
The spouse-psychologists Arthur and Elaine Aron came up with the 36 questions two people could ask one another that could make them fall in love – anyone, even strangers. Some questions are closed but searching (“Before making a telephone call, do you ever rehearse what you’re going to say? Why?”), while others are open (“What do you most value in a friendship?”). That was back in 1997, and three decades of speed dating have cast some doubt on the inevitability of love as the outcome of the process (which, to be fair, the Arons never claimed), but the idea has endured that questioning itself creates intimacy, symmetrical questioning is more intimate still, and open-ended questions flip you into a more vulnerable, receptive frame.
The philosopher Peter Worley devised the question X manoeuvre, a closed question followed by an open one. “The first is the easier to answer,” Watson explains, “and once you’ve committed yourself to that, you’re happier and more comfortable exploring the area around it.”
It sounds so simple as to be self-evident, but try it for yourself, and try the counterfactual. If someone bowled up with the question: “Do you enjoy what you do?” there’s something simultaneously condescending about it (“Little man, have you found satisfaction in your pursuits?”) and faux naive (“What is this thing called adulthood? Is it enjoyable?”). Try the X technique – “What do you do? Do you enjoy it?” – and not only does the second question follow more naturally from the first, but it gives you the impression that your first answer was interesting enough to have spurred the second.
![Lani Watson standing by the river in Leith, Edinburgh](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b87958d1c669197d5dd17beb4c487651e10ea3d3/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Question Y is the “divergent” sequence, starting with something easy, closed (“Did you vote in the referendum?”), then following up with something more open, likely to provoke difference but in a precinct you have already established as friendly – “Do you think referendums are a good idea?” Question Z is a line of inquiry that will change direction or the tightness of its focus over its course (think of the shape of a Z). I’m not wild about Watson’s example (“Do you like chocolate?”; “Given that coffee also comes from a bean, doesn’t it follow that you also like coffee?”), but you can see the potential: for unpredictability, as well as a certain inviting quality – part of what puts people off being questioned is the thought that they will be wrong or humiliated. A set of questions that slaloms all over the place is unlikely to have right answers.
Unavoidably, questioning feels as if it drives towards politics of a certain kind. If, as Watson writes, cognitive closure is heightened by stress and drives in-group identification and, with it, suspicion of others, then breaking out of it with a questioning disposition would send you in the other direction, towards (broadly) philosophies of unity and hope. “I really take seriously the project of trying to write for a very broad audience,” Watson says, “so I want to be in a politically neutral space, which is not where I am myself, personally.”
Right, I say. You literally have blue hair. Kemi Badenoch would probably write a speech about you. Unavoidably, she says, “a questioning mindset will bring us a lot closer together, wherever we are, because essentially you’re just opening up space to explore the possibility that you’re wrong about something. That you might not know what you thought you knew.”
It’s a mistake, though, to think curiosity and certainty are utterly at odds, let alone that the first has a monopoly on harmony and the second drives division. “You build curiosity by coming to be an expert and pushing yourself to the edge of your knowledge. So certainty and curiosity can’t be diametrically opposed in that way, because you build curiosity on a foundation of certainties. But there is also a dynamic where you can close down curiosity by being certain.” Nor is she saying that there’s no value in knowledge: “Answers are good; we do need answers. That’s just not my job.”
One of the first examples Watson writes about, almost the definitive question whose purpose doesn’t lie in an answer, is from a therapist: “What is the one thing now that you want to be able to do in the future?” It has elements of a few of those 36 questions to make you fall in love – inviting what might be a painful reckoning with reality, softened by the branching possibilities of the future, and the knowledge of your own agency (the more parlour-game version of this is, “What would you do if you had 12 months to live? Why aren’t you doing it now?”).
“You find a new understanding as an exclusive result of that question,” Watson says, “but not because you’re secretly answering it in your head. That’s a big part of the reason why therapy is such an effective form of healing, because you could ask yourself a bunch of questions and try to solve your own issues, but only someone else can ask a question that you weren’t expecting, push you into a different space and make you feel cared for.”
If interpersonal instances land the most convincingly or recognisably, the credit Watson pays to the question reaches back into decisions we could only guess at, and out into realms we can’t know. “I started to think about what encouraged human migration out of Africa,” she says. “Could it have been that questioning: ‘What’s around the corner? What’s over the horizon?’ The combination of curiosity and exploration, but also the capacity to form those into questions, is integral to moving out and moving forward.” It sounds likely, but we cannot know it for certain. “If you’re just interested in the answers, you are missing out on a form of power,” she says, which is as certain as you’ll find Watson about anything.
guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
summary: Philosopher Lani Watson explores the power and hidden value of asking questions in a world dominated by an obsession with final answers. In her book, Q, she outlines the different stages of questioning—from proto-questioning in animals to complex social communication in humans—and explains how adopting a questioning mindset stimulates dopamine and fosters curiosity. By learning to embrace "aporia," or the state of confusion, individuals can break free from the desire for cognitive closure and open themselves up to deeper exploration and connection.
key_points: Asking questions stimulates dopamine and activates brain reward circuitry regardless of whether an answer is found, encouraging environmental exploration.
Watson categorizes questioning into four stages: proto-questioning, private questioning, social questioning, and spoken questioning.
Modern society leans heavily toward an answer-oriented mindset due to educational metrics, social norms, and the desire for cognitive closure.
Techniques like "assumption mining" and structured questioning sequences (such as the question X or Y maneuvers) help build intimacy and reduce the fear of being wrong.

title: New ibuprofen warning as painkiller linked to hormone changes - AOL
author: Neil Shaw
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Millions take ibuprofen regularly](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/d3b11eaa-e6d5-375e-9a46-817f53a6e4c7/83720848-92e1-4537-b8ca-98ca694ba487.jpg)
Anyone who regularly takes a common over-the-counter painkiller has been warned it could have serious side effects.
Ibuprofen is one of the UK's most commonly taken painkillers as some people take it every day for weeks or months without thinking of themselves as regular medicine users.Regular ibuprofen use has been linked to changes in male reproductive hormones, while a separate study of sister NSAIDs found temporary effects on ovulation and progesterone in women.
Both can be missed because the person taking the tablets may not feel an obvious change, according toMike Kocsis, founder ofBalance My Hormones.
![The pills are easily available in the UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/d3b11eaa-e6d5-375e-9a46-817f53a6e4c7/7bb05195-cb63-4e07-895e-bf709e2f5a20.jpg)
A US study found young men given the maximum daily amount of ibuprofen for six weeks saw a rise in their luteinising hormone (LH) while the testosterone-to-LH ratio fell, a state the paper called compensated hypogonadism. MrKocsissaid: “Compensated hypogonadism means the testes are underperforming, but testosterone can still look normal because the brain is pushing the system harder to hold it steady.
"The worrying part is not that hormone levels crashed. It is that they stayed normal because the body was masking the problem by pushing harder, which is exactly why a regular user would never feel it happening. A system forced to compensate long term has less in reserve.”
A separate randomised clinical study with women tested diclofenac, naproxen and etoricoxib, painkillers from the same NSAID family, taken continuously for 10 days in the middle of the cycle. It tested sister drugs, not ibuprofen itself.
![It can alter your hormones if taken for a sustained period](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/d3b11eaa-e6d5-375e-9a46-817f53a6e4c7/32b81a06-ffe6-4ba6-a9cf-792339b92517.jpg)
Ovulation was drastically reduced, by about 93 per cent with diclofenac and about 75 per cent with naproxen. Progesterone fell significantly. Ovulation returned to normal after stopping.
MrKocsis said: “Ovulation is a hormonal event, and blocking the prostaglandins that trigger it can scramble the cycle's hormone pattern while the drugs are being taken. Ibuprofen works through the same prostaglandin-blocking mechanism, which is why the issue is relevant to women too.”
Standard NHS medicines guidance generally cautions against NSAIDs for women trying to conceive and during pregnancy, although the exact advice depends on the specific drug and stage of pregnancy.
MrKocsis said: “An occasional dose for a headache or a strain is not the issue, and nobody should panic about normal use. Never stop a prescribed anti-inflammatory without speaking to the prescriber. Paracetamol is an alternative for many everyday aches where it is suitable. Anyone relying on ibuprofen daily should mention it to a pharmacist or GP. Anyone worried about symptoms of low testosterone or cycle problems should get hormone levels properly tested rather than guessing.”
summary: Regular use of the common painkiller ibuprofen has been linked to potential changes in male reproductive hormones, according to a recent warning. A US study found that young men taking maximum daily doses experienced compensated hypogonadism, where the body masks underperforming testes by increasing brain stimulation. Additionally, a separate study on related NSAID painkillers showed temporary reductions in ovulation and progesterone levels in women.
key_points: Ibuprofen is one of the most commonly taken painkillers in the UK, often used daily for weeks or months.
A US study found that young men taking maximum daily ibuprofen for six weeks developed compensated hypogonadism.
Related NSAID painkillers taken by women caused drastically reduced ovulation and significantly lower progesterone levels, which returned to normal after stopping.
Experts emphasize that occasional doses for headaches are not an issue, but individuals relying on daily ibuprofen should consult a pharmacist or GP.

title: ‘Clear red flags’ missed by Highland GP whose patient died from pancreatic cancer
author: Philip Murray
content:
Highland GP practice ordered to apologise by Scottish Public Service Ombudsman (SPSO) after ‘clear red flags’ were missed in diagnosing a patient who later died of pancreatic cancer
![](https://www.inverness-courier.co.uk/_assets/twitterx.png)
![Google](https://www.inverness-courier.co.uk/_assets/gpref.jpg)
“Clear red flags” for cancer were missed by a Highland GP surgery months before their patient died from pancreatic cancer.
The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman (SPSO) said the practice, which has not been named, had “not immediately followed up” on the possibility of cancer even after the patient had raised it as a possibility when their symptoms persisted.
By the time that scans confirmed the patient’s cancer prognosis, they only had six weeks left to live.
And the SPSO has now ordered the unnamed practice to apologise to the spouse of the patient, following a ruling this week that there were “missed opportunities” to diagnose them sooner.
The spouse, referred to only as ‘C’, complained to the ombudsman over the standard of care and treatment provided to their late partner.
Their partner, referred to as ‘A’, had gone to the GP practice after experiencing “steady unexplained weight loss”.
But despite the practice diagnosing ‘A’ with diabetes and prescribing medication, their symptoms persisted “over the following months”.
At this point ‘A’ queried “the possibility of pancreatic cancer with the GP”, but the SPSO said this “was not immediately followed up by the GP”.
When ‘A’ continued to experience symptoms, the GP sent an urgent referral to gastroenterologists - specialists in stomach and intestine disorders - and the following month the GP sent a “new urgent suspicion of cancer referral after blood tests showed a change in A’s liver function”.
The SPSO said that it was only then, following a CT scan that ‘A’ was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. They died just six weeks later.
Following their death, A’s spouse complained that there was an unreasonable delay in recognising that their specific symptoms indicated they may have had pancreatic cancer. They also complained that there was an unreasonable delay in referring A to appropriate secondary care for further investigation.
In its ruling, the SPSO said: “We found that relevant guidance was clear that A had red flag symptoms for pancreatic cancer from their initial presentation.
“From this point until the urgent suspicion of cancer referral, there were missed opportunities to recognise the significance of A’s symptoms and refer them onward for further investigation. Given this, we upheld both of these complaints.”
The SPSO added that C had also complained that the practice had “failed to provide reasonable input” into A’s palliative care following their terminal diagnosis.
“We found that there was a lack of proactive planning and communication on the part of the practice,” ruled the SPSO. “Therefore, we upheld this complaint.”
They continued: “Finally, C complained that there was an unreasonable reliance on telephone consultations. We accepted that telephone consultations are an important part of delivering a GP service. However, in A’s case, we concluded that face-to-face appointments may have resulted in less delay in diagnosis and a better quality of end-of-life care. On balance, we upheld this complaint.
“Although we upheld all of C’s complaints, we did note that the practice had responded constructively to the concerns raised and our enquiries. We asked the practice to apologise to C but made no further recommendations given the action already taken.”
Following its ruling, the SPSO has told the GP surgery to apologise to C for the “unreasonable delay in recognising that A’s specific symptoms indicated they may have had pancreatic cancer and referring A to appropriate secondary care for further investigation”.
They also told it to “apologise to C for the unreasonable standard of end-of-life and palliative care input provided to A” and to ”apologise to C for the unreasonable reliance on telephone consultations in their interactions with A.”
It concluded: “We have asked the organisation to provide us with evidence that they have implemented the recommendations we have made on this case by the deadline we set.”
summary: The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman ordered an unnamed Highland GP practice to apologize after missing clear red flags for pancreatic cancer in a patient who presented with unexplained weight loss. Despite the patient suggesting the possibility of cancer when symptoms persisted, the practice delayed referrals until scans confirmed a terminal diagnosis, leaving the patient with only six weeks to live. The ombudsman upheld all complaints from the patient's spouse regarding delayed diagnosis, inadequate palliative care planning, and an unreasonable reliance on telephone consultations.
key_points: A Highland GP practice missed red flag symptoms for pancreatic cancer after a patient presented with steady unexplained weight loss.
The practice failed to immediately follow up when the patient themselves raised the possibility of pancreatic cancer.
By the time a CT scan confirmed the cancer diagnosis following urgent referrals, the patient had only six weeks left to live.
The Scottish Public Services Ombudsman upheld complaints regarding delayed diagnosis, lack of proactive palliative care planning, and reliance on telephone consultations.
The practice has been ordered to issue formal apologies to the patient's spouse.

title: Ebola outbreak ‘growing faster, wider’ as DRC death toll passes 2,500: UN
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![(FILES) Volunteers of the Democratic Republic of Congo Red Cross wearing personal protective equipment carry the body of an Ebola virus disease victim from the morgue of the Rwampara health centre, Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of Congo, on June 8, 2026 before loading it into a vehicle for transfer to a cemetery as part of safe and dignified burial operations aimed at preventing the spread of the virus.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a7de8a1f313-1786636450.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Ebola virus continues spreading “exponentially” in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the United Nations has warned.
Sounding the alarm that the outbreak is “spreading faster and wider” than ever before, the UN’s Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis reported that more than 2,500 people have now died.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak ‘global emergency’ as infections pass 5,000: WHO
- list 2 of 3How Ebola became the deadliest outbreak in DR Congo’s history
- list 3 of 3DR Congo to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine as Ebola infections surge
The official called for more funds to be put to work to try to control the spread, noting that the existing pool of money will run out within weeks.
Efforts to stem the epidemic since the outbreak began in May have faced several challenges.
Conflict and a lack of government control and infrastructure in the eastern DRC have disrupted the effort. Where health workers – many of whom have died after contracting the virus – and facilities are able to operate, they have come under attack by frustrated and frightened locals, Harneis said.
More than 260 attacks on health workers have been reported in the past six months, and eight health workers have been killed. More than 160 healthcare workers have fallen ill, with 43 dying.
Aid workers have said many locals believe conspiracy theories that the outbreak is a hoax, and have reacted angrily when health restrictions prevent them from personally burying loved ones.
Efforts to control the outbreak have also been complicated by the lack of a vaccine for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which causes severe haemorrhagic fever.
Existing security concerns are also hampering the battle to stop the spread.
“All of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs,” Harneis said.
The UN official warned the epidemic could spread to neighbouring countries without a ramped-up response, and urged more staffing and resources to reach remote areas.
summary: The United Nations has warned that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading exponentially, with the death toll surpassing 2,500. Efforts to control the epidemic are severely hampered by ongoing conflict, attacks on health workers, a lack of funding, conspiracy theories among locals, and the absence of a vaccine for the rare Bundibugyo strain. UN officials are urging for increased resources, staffing, and international support to prevent the virus from spreading to neighboring countries.
key_points: The DRC Ebola death toll has exceeded 2,500, with the UN warning the outbreak is growing faster and wider.
Health workers and facilities have faced over 260 attacks in six months, resulting in multiple deaths among medical staff.
Response efforts are hindered by conflict, a lack of infrastructure, conspiracy theories, and anger over burial restrictions.
There is currently no vaccine available for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus driving infections.
Existing funding is expected to run out within weeks, and the UN has called for urgent additional resources.

title: New Aldi 99p food item coming out Thursday helps lower high blood pressure - AOL
author: Charlotte Smith
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![A customer leaves an Aldi Stores](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/17ab2edd-0c12-38da-a549-0e3e6f408722/39828773-5fc8-4b56-ba51-9c06773393d5.jpg)
Aldi is bringing out a food item next week as part of a new Special Buy offer that costs less than £1 and may also help reduce the risk of high blood pressure. Scientific research shows that the ingredients in the food item are rich in a key mineral and help ease the strain on blood vessel walls.
On Thursday next week, August 27, Aldi will be bringing out a new Fiesta Red Gazpacho Soup for 99p, as part of its upcoming Taste Of Spain range. The "fresh and vibrant" ingredients include ripe tomatoes, peppers, cucumber, olive oil and garlic.
Gazpacho is best served chilled. Heating store-bought gazpacho destroys the delicate vitamin C and enzymes that contribute to its heart-healthy properties.
A large clinical study published in Nutrition, Metabolism and Cardiovascular Diseases tracked nearly 4,000 adults and found that regular consumption of gazpacho can reduce the risk of high blood pressure by 27%. The researchers also found that the raw ingredients work together so well that they can cancel out the bad effects of the extra salt often added to store-bought versions.
![Aldi's new Fiesta Red Gazpacho Soup for 99p](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/17ab2edd-0c12-38da-a549-0e3e6f408722/757f5316-a3e8-4561-bacd-499565430db2.jpg)
How does Aldi's soup ingredients work together to lower high blood pressure?
The raw garlic, onions, and tomatoes in gazpacho boost nitric oxide production in your body. Nitric oxide relaxes and widens your blood vessels, which directly reduces arterial pressure.
Tomatoes, cucumbers, and red peppers are naturally rich in potassium. Potassium helps your kidneys flush out excess sodium, easing the strain on your blood vessel walls.
In addition, the high concentrations of vitamin C, carotenes, and polyphenols help prevent inflammation and keep your arteries flexible. Researchers found that the mix of these fresh, uncooked ingredients works together in a way that is stronger than the bad effects of any extra salt usually added to the soup.
To reduce blood pressure, you can make simple changes such as eating less salt, working out for 150 minutes each week, shedding some extra pounds, increasing your intake of fruits and vegetables, and cutting back on alcohol and caffeine. You can check the NHS High Blood Pressure Guidelines for more medical information.
![Bowl with Andalusian gazpacho and ingredients](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/17ab2edd-0c12-38da-a549-0e3e6f408722/15fdbaf9-117c-4faa-970d-f1abf254fca4.jpg)
Important considerations
People with hypertension are typically told to avoid store-bought soups due to sodium. Aldi's gazpacho formulas generally contain between 0.7g to 0.79g of salt per 100g (yielding about 0.7g of salt per half-pack serving).
While this is a moderate amount of salt, the researchers at the University of Barcelona noted that the overall bioactive synergy between the raw vegetables and olive oil outweighs the salt content. The soup remains highly cardio-protective.
Stick to the recommended half-carton serving size to keep your sodium intake under control. Avoid adding croutons or extra salt before serving. Instead, kick up the flavour with fresh ground black pepper, a squeeze of fresh lemon, or fresh basil.
High blood pressure is bad because it forces your heart to work too hard and puts too much force on your artery walls. Over time, this constant extra strain damages your blood vessels and vital organs, raising your risk for life-threatening issues like heart attacks, strokes, and kidney failure.
Where does gazpacho originate from?
Gazpacho comes from Andalusia, in southern Spain. The first version was brought by Roman soldiers and only had bread, water, vinegar, garlic, and olive oil. Field workers would mash these ingredients together in a wooden mortar to make a cool, refreshing paste on hot summer days.
For many years, gazpacho didn't have tomatoes or peppers. It wasn't until the 16th century, when Spanish explorers returned from the Americas, that tomatoes and green peppers were added.
summary: Aldi is launching a 99p Fiesta Red Gazpacho Soup as part of its Taste Of Spain range on Thursday, August 27. Scientific research suggests that regular consumption of gazpacho, made with fresh raw vegetables like tomatoes and peppers, can help reduce the risk of high blood pressure. The soup should be served chilled to preserve its heart-healthy nutrients, vitamins, and enzymes.
key_points: Aldi is releasing its Fiesta Red Gazpacho Soup for 99p on Thursday, August 27.
A study of nearly 4,000 adults found regular gazpacho consumption can reduce high blood pressure risk by 27%.
Raw ingredients like garlic, onions, and tomatoes boost nitric oxide to relax blood vessels.
Potassium from tomatoes, cucumbers, and red peppers helps kidneys flush out excess sodium.
Gazpacho should be served chilled because heating store-bought versions destroys delicate vitamin C and heart-healthy enzymes.

title: Measles outbreak in Worcestershire exposes hospital vaccine gaps
author: James Pearson
content:
![A blonde nurse with protective coverings on her face, hands and chest holds up a needle and vaccine vial.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/549/cpsprodpb/97d6/live/f565d1f0-9c7a-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
A rise in measles cases in the West Midlands has sparked calls for people to get themselves and their children protected against the disease
- Published
Hundreds of front line NHS staff have received the MMR jab, following an "unprecedented" outbreak of measles at a Worcestershire hospital.
In May, seven positive cases of the highly contagious disease were reported at Worcestershire Royal.
Vulnerable patients - including a pregnant woman - required preventative medicine, while some unvaccinated staff had to isolate for 21 days.
Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust said a review of 8,500 staff had revealed that more than a quarter in patient-facing roles had not been vaccinated or lacked natural immunity. More than 400 have now received the jab.
The three-month measles, external outbreak, which was declared over on 24 July, was described as "unprecedented" by the Worcestershire Acute's quality governance committee.
According to the hospital trust's board papers for July, external, the infections included two members of staff working on a higher risk ward.
Three vulnerable hospital patients - a pregnant woman and two patients who had received organ transplants - received Human Normal Immunoglobulin, a preventative medicine containing antibodies to fight infection.
Contact tracing was carried out to identify how many people may have been infected. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said cases were also identified in the community.
At the time of the outbreak, Dame Julie Moore, a non-executive director at the trust, expressed concern about "the lack of a robust process" for checking the vaccination status of staff.
July's board papers detail how she also "raised the patient safety implications of unvaccinated clinical staff".
![Portrait photograph of Dame Julie Moore wearing a light blue jacket and blue-framed glasses.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/86af/live/bfe0be50-9bbc-11f1-ae8a-8d57110c5ba6.jpg)
Dame Julie Moore raised concerns about the monitoring of staff vaccination status and the potential implications for patient safety
Measles cases have been on the rise in the West Midlands.
So far this year, 29 cases have been recorded in Worcestershire, according to UKHSA.
These include 16 cases between 11 May and 8 June.
In 2026, England has registered two deaths to children as a result of measles.
"Measles can spread quickly among those who are unvaccinated and can cause serious complications especially in young children, pregnant women and those with weakened immune systems," said Emma Booth, consultant in health protection and the vaccine lead for UKHSA West Midlands.
"We encourage all adults to check they have had two doses of MMR or contact their GP surgery if they are unsure, and book an appointment for any doses missed," she said.
Simon Adams, the chair of patient advocacy group Healthwatch Worcestershire, said: "It's really disappointing to hear that the hospital could be, if you like, such a hotspot.
"If we go into hospitals, as patients, we want to be safe. If you work in a hospital, in whatever role, you want to be safe. And the way of being safe is being vaccinated."
He added the trust had an obligation to make sure staff in a patient-facing role were vaccinated.
No legal requirement
In a statement, the trust said: "In terms of our staff we follow national guidelines around vaccinations."
To work inside the NHS, all frontline and clinical healthcare workers are recommended by NHS England to have documented evidence of two MMR doses or positive immunity.
However, there is currently no mandatory legal requirement.
As part of its response to the outbreak, the trust said on-site vaccine clinics had boosted the percentage of vaccinated patient-facing staff from 72% to 94%.
It said it had also "strengthened oversight and monitoring" of staff immunisation, including reviewing pre-employment checks and requiring volunteers and work experience placements to show evidence of vaccination.
Follow BBC Hereford & Worcester on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external.
summary: An unprecedented measles outbreak at Worcestershire Royal Hospital involving seven positive cases prompted hundreds of frontline NHS staff to receive the MMR vaccine. A review revealed that more than a quarter of patient-facing staff lacked vaccination or natural immunity, leading to criticisms regarding staff vetting and patient safety. The three-month outbreak was declared over on July 24, and the trust has since strengthened oversight and monitoring of staff immunisation.
key_points: Seven positive measles cases were reported at Worcestershire Royal Hospital in May, leading to a three-month outbreak that ended on July 24.
A hospital review found that over a quarter of patient-facing staff lacked vaccination or natural immunity, prompting more than 400 to receive the jab.
Vulnerable individuals, including a pregnant woman and two organ transplant patients, required preventative medicine, while unvaccinated staff faced 21-day isolation.
There is currently no mandatory legal requirement for NHS healthcare workers to be vaccinated for MMR, though it is recommended by NHS England.
Following the outbreak, the trust improved the percentage of vaccinated patient-facing staff from 72% to 94% and strengthened pre-employment vaccination checks.

title: DRC Ebola outbreak 'growing exponentially,' UN says
author: Natalie Muller
content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is "growing exponentially" and risks spilling over into neighboring countries unless containment efforts are stepped up, the UN's senior Ebola coordinator said Friday.
The outbreak is already the deadliest in the country's history, with more than 2,500 deaths from over 5,000 infections.
"The epidemic is spreading widely. It's now covering an area that is bigger than France," UN senior Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis told journalists, adding that half of the 2,500 deaths had been reported in the last 20 days alone.
"It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response."
He stressed that aid funding and the delivery of resources to remote areas needed to be urgently ramped up to slow and eventually stop the virus's transmission.
"If we do not ... then this epidemic will become more deadly. It will spread wider and it risks to spread into neighboring countries," Harneis added.
Fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.
The first infections were detected earlier this year in the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, an area where armed groups operate and health infrastructure is poor. The virus has since spread to five other provinces as well as to neighboring Uganda.
Congolese authorities officially declared an Ebola outbreak on May 15, but experts believe the virus may have already been circulating for some time before that point.
Officials say it is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is expanding about three times faster than the 2014-2016 outbreak in West Africa — the world's deadliest on record— which killed around 11,000 people.
Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.
DRC to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo Ebola vaccine
Meanwhile, the World Health Organization has announced it will immediately release 70,000 doses of Merck's Ervebo Ebola vaccine to the DRC in a bid to help contain the epidemic.
The Ervebo shot has only been approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, although the WHO said in a statement that early data from animal trials showed it may also give some protection against Bundibugyo — the strain behind the current epidemic.
"The allocation includes 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus, and 50,000 doses for frontline and health workers," the UN health agency said.
Edited by: Zac Crellin
Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.
summary: The UN reports that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is growing exponentially and risks spreading to neighboring countries without increased containment efforts and aid funding. The epidemic has become the deadliest in the country's history, covering an area larger than France with over 2,500 deaths from more than 5,000 infections. In response, the WHO is releasing 70,000 doses of Merck's Ervebo vaccine for frontline workers and clinical trials.
key_points: The DRC Ebola outbreak is expanding faster than the response and risks spilling into neighboring countries.
The epidemic has caused over 2,500 deaths from more than 5,000 infections, covering an area larger than France.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare Ebola type lacking an approved vaccine or treatment.
The WHO is allocating 70,000 doses of Merck's Ervebo vaccine for health workers and clinical trials.
Officials report the outbreak is expanding about three times faster than the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic.

title: Under-fives and pregnant women told to avoid runny eggs when eating out over salmonella risk
author: Nick Triggle; Hugh Pym
content:
![Plate with runny eggs](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d127/live/9710c0e0-9d53-11f1-aac2-870643eea2ac.jpg)
- Published
Vulnerable people are being warned not to eat under-cooked or runny eggs when they are eating out because of the developing salmonella outbreak.
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) told the BBC the under fives, over 65s, women who are pregnant and those with health conditions should avoid them along with freshly-made products that might contain uncooked eggs, such as mayonnaise, souffle and hollandaise sauce.
But the FSA said well-cooked eggs in restaurants, cafes and from takeaways were fine to eat.
It comes after the UK Health Security Agency declared a national outbreak of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill.
It is thought imported eggs or dishes containing them are behind the outbreak.
FSA chief scientific adviser Ian Young said: "If people are eating out or consuming eggs or egg-containing products from cafes and restaurants then for those people in particular who are young, elderly, pregnant or vulnerable, it's important to make sure that any eggs or egg products that you consume in those settings have been very well cooked."
But he reiterated the message that it was fine for people to buy British eggs from supermarkets as chickens bred here are vaccinated against common strains of salmonella.
"There is no link to those eggs to this current outbreak."
He described the outbreak as "unusually large and rapidly increasing".
"People need to be careful," he added.
Greatest risk
There have been over 200 cases in the UK linked to this outbreak. The majority are across England.
Genetic testing suggests all the infections are part of the same outbreak and there are similarities with previous outbreaks involving imported eggs.
Investigations into individual cases also suggest the eateries involved were buying eggs from abroad.
Salmonella are a family of bacteria that typically live harmlessly in the digestive tract of animals including cattle, pigs and chicken - which is why eggs and poultry are among foods commonly associated with the infection.
People can catch it by eating contaminated food that has not been cooked properly, or cross contamination after mixing raw and cooked food in the kitchen or coming into contact with infected animals.
It can then cause stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. In most cases people recover without further help but older people, babies and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk of severe disease.
Hospital care with fluids and sometimes antibiotics can help in these cases.
Anyone who is concerned is being advised to contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.
summary: Vulnerable groups, including pregnant women and children under five, are being advised to avoid runny eggs and uncooked egg products when eating out due to a national salmonella outbreak. The Food Standards Agency recommends that these individuals only consume well-cooked eggs in restaurants and cafes. The outbreak, which has caused over 200 cases and one death, is believed to be linked to imported eggs rather than British supermarket eggs.
key_points: A national salmonella outbreak has resulted in over 200 cases and one death in the UK.
Vulnerable groups should avoid runny or under-cooked eggs and related dishes when eating out.
Investigations and genetic testing suggest imported eggs are behind the outbreak.
British eggs from supermarkets remain considered safe as UK chickens are vaccinated against common salmonella strains.
Salmonella infection can cause symptoms such as stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever.

title: Ebola outbreak: five big questions
author: Kat Lay
content:
Almost 100 days ago, Africa’s public health watchdog reported an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
There have now been almost 5,000 cases and more than 2,000 deaths since 15 May, making this Ebola outbreak the biggest and most deadly in the DRC’s history.
It is on course to be “the largest one in the world”, according to Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), speaking at a press briefing in mid August.
Why are case and death figures still increasing?
The outbreak was declared on 15 May, but is thought to have been spreading unreported for months before that date. That means “the outbreak had a big head start, it is still way ahead of us and we are playing catch-up,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said last week.
The Bundibugyo virus causing the latest outbreak is a rarer type of the Ebola disease, and has no licensed vaccine or medicine. That means health workers trying to bring the outbreak under control must rely on painstaking efforts to identify cases, isolate them for treatment, and then also identify their contacts for monitoring.
![A line of people waiting on the shore near a boat. Health workers in blue PPE attend to them.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/421ad51e10136ff59b5321189be36b661cc96525/0_0_3811_2541/master/3811.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Uganda did that successfully after travellers from the DRC imported the virus. It declared its outbreak over after just 20 cases and two deaths.
But in Ituri and North Kivu, the DRC provinces with the highest numbers of cases, and where armed conflict has displaced tens of thousands of people, officials have been unable to identify enough contacts to get on top of transmission. Africa CDC estimates the response is tracing about 12% of contacts – the target is 95%.
Authorities are now switching to a new approach that will see them going door to door to seek people with symptoms, and appointing people in every village to be part of the response effort.
Where are the 850 people who tested positive but are unaccounted for?
As of 15 August, there had been 4,945 confirmed cases, with 730 people in treatment centres, 1,040 people recorded as surviving the virus, and 2,325 deaths.
That leaves 850 people who have tested positive, but are unaccounted for in the number of patients, survivors and victims. People who have the virus, but whose whereabouts are unknown, represent a high risk of onward Ebola transmission.
In the hardest-hit areas, many locals have extremely little trust in the authorities. They ask why the government is suddenly present, when communities had been struggling alone before – including with other diseases such as cholera and malaria.
![People digging and panning in muddy water at an open-cast goldmine.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6786aa637dc7e4e509cf2cf17eb5bbc7d279d3c6/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Mistrust translates into infected people coming forward for treatment late, if at all – and sometimes, fleeing Ebola treatment centres because they do not trust that they will get the necessary care there.
Some families prefer to care for their loved ones at home – and, if they die, to follow their usual burial practices that involve touching the bodies. Ebola is spread through body fluids, and carers without the proper protective equipment face a high risk of infection.
Is money that has been promised reaching the frontline?
The availability of banknotes has been a real issue for paying workers involved in the response. The airport in Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, has been closed to commercial flights for months, making it harder to bring cash in.
In remote areas, there are no banks and mobile money systems are unavailable, says Prof Yap Boum, of Africa CDC. “The frontline responders, the community healthcare workers, the people working in treatment centres […] you need to pay them with cash.
“If you don’t have the cash in the city, and therefore in those villages, it’s difficult to run some operations,” he says.
Some staff, including nurses and the teams in charge of safe burials, have gone on strike over the lack of pay. In the face of attacks from the community, many of whom do not believe the Ebola outbreak is even real, they say they “see no point in risking our lives” without compensation.
![A health worker wearing PPE sits on the ground in the street, with an arm raised in protest. A crowd of people stand behind him.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4e7f8a4e5b8ed3824129c30baa972d88d591a208/0_0_5000_2813/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The new, village-based approach that goes from door to door will need more workers and probably be more expensive than the approach up to now.
However, officials have insisted that payment problems are being ironed out.
Africa CDC says $518m (£382m) is needed for the direct health response to Ebola, and another $882m to tackle surrounding humanitarian issues.
Donors including the US, EU, African Union member states, the World Bank and its Pandemic Fund have pledged more than enough to cover that amount – but not all the funding has been released. Tedros said last week that only $264m of the $518m had been disbursed. Getting ahead of the outbreak, he warned, “depends on financing”.
Do we have any treatments or vaccines available?
In the wake of Covid-19, the world launched an ambitious initiative to make diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines available within 100 days of any future pandemic. And while Ebola is not a pandemic, the International Pandemic Preparedness Secretariat has been tracking progress on that basis. The world is not going to meet the 100-day deadline – but there has been progress.
Testing is now available in labs in Ituri, rather than requiring samples to be sent to Kinshasa for confirmation.
![Hands wearing protective blue surgical gloves holding a test tube.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ad2c30fb5108df57d87abc38322b0abd9e18d77f/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Safety trials have begun of two vaccines designed specifically to protect against the Bundibugyo strain. And new evidence suggests that an existing Ebola vaccine called Ervebo, designed to fight the Zaire strain of the virus, may offer enough cross-protection against Bundibugyo to cut death rates, even if it does not prevent infection – officials are planning to roll it out on that basis.
Trials have begun on some drugs both as treatment and as prophylaxis when given to someone exposed to a Bundibugyo patient.
In the coming months, the cost and access to any drugs or vaccines that prove successful in trials are likely to be a test of international solidarity.
What will things look like in another 100 days?
The outbreak will not be over by the start of December. But WHO officials hope a renewed focus, and shifting their approach to actively seeking cases on a village-by-village basis will reverse the spread of the disease in the DRC within three months.
One early indicator of progress would be a fall in the case-fatality rate – the proportion of people testing positive who die, which has risen in recent weeks. As of 15 August, it stood at 47%.
![A woman, whose face is out of shot, lies on a bed with a stent in her hand.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6911747cc2f9256438dac5b99b938fa485da47db/0_0_5897_3931/master/5897.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
A high death rate is likely to reflect people coming forward late, when it is harder for doctors to treat them, and cases not being reported. A fall would suggest improvements in tracing efforts, as well as potentially better treatment.
Another key thing to watch for is any further spread to neighbouring countries – South Sudan, which neighbours Ituri, has its own ongoing humanitarian crisis that would make a response to Ebola harder. Authorities in the country have been stepping up surveillance, including by training health workers in border towns to spot signs and symptoms of the disease.
Potential vaccines and treatments, and an intensified response, are reasons to be hopeful. But if current efforts fail to bear fruit, the outbreak is on course to surpass the biggest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people in west Africa between 2014 and 2016.
summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is facing the biggest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, with nearly 5,000 cases and over 2,000 deaths recorded since May. Public health officials are struggling to contain the virus due to armed conflict, community mistrust, and severe shortages of frontline cash to pay workers. Authorities are now shifting to a door-to-door village approach and testing new vaccines and treatments to curb the spread.
key_points: The outbreak is driven by the rarer Bundibugyo virus, which currently lacks a licensed vaccine or medicine.
Armed conflict in Ituri and North Kivu has hindered contact tracing, with only about 12% of contacts currently tracked compared to a 95% target.
There are 850 people who tested positive but remain unaccounted for, increasing the risk of onward transmission.
Frontline healthcare workers have gone on strike due to a lack of physical cash to pay wages in remote areas.
Safety trials have begun for new vaccines targeting the Bundibugyo strain, and officials plan to roll out the existing Ervebo vaccine for cross-protection.

title: Why we shouldn’t take advice from biohackers like Bryan Johnson
author: Richard Godwin
content:
Another classic Dantean contrapasso: the misers were forced to push giant boulders around a semi-circular track with their chests for the sin of hoarding all their money. When they reached the end, they would crash into the spendthrifts, themselves forced to push a boulder around their own semi-circular track for the sin of wasting all their money. The intended meaning of this punishment was to underline the importance of moderation – a message that doesn’t necessarily cut through today, though perhaps it should.
I speak to Christian Collins, a private GP based in Oxfordshire, who practises what he calls “medical wellness”. (He is on Instagram, as it happens, but has hardly any followers, which is reassuring in a GP.) His interest in “wellness” began after he was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in his 30s, following years of stress, weight gain and poor eating habits. As a doctor, he knew what was in store: a lifetime of medication. Instead, he changed his diet, sleep, mindset and exercise, and says that within 12 weeks he had returned to normal blood-sugar levels without medication. “At medical school we’re taught this concept of the medical model, which is sometimes very simplistic,” he tells me. “You have a symptom, then you take a history and examination, then you do an investigation, and then you give a person something to essentially reverse that condition. But medicine conventionally doesn’t really think much about prevention.”
It also doesn’t have much to say about how you feel, he says. “Without being too cynical about conventional medicine, what the NHS will do for you if you’re a 70-year-old man with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, gout and a bit of type 2 diabetes is put you on eight or nine different medications. And they’re not there to make you feel any better; they’re just there to keep you alive for as many years as that allows.”
The way he sees it, the great difference between medicine and wellness can be summed up in one word: evidence. However, just because there’s an absence of evidence, it doesn’t mean there’s evidence of that absence, he reasons, and if it is not harming a patient, then why not give, for example, magnesium supplements a try? “There are lots of Instagrammable hospital doctors who will make videos looking at papers on, say, magnesium and say: ‘There’s no evidence for that. I’m going to debunk you,’” he says. “Whereas I know that some of my patients say it works wonders for their muscle cramps. It does a great job for sleep and has no harm on their heart function. There may be no evidence. It may be a placebo. But I’m doing no harm, and I’m helping my patients.”
Everyone is selling something. Still, Collins tells me that his more usual advice is not to take extra things but simply to do less. The overall problem is that we are living in a culture of extraordinary abundance that is making us unwell. Indeed, a society organised around perpetual consumption and economic growth is fundamentally at odds with the things that actually sustain wellbeing: family, sleep, exercise, good food, time and human connection.
“I see my most apparently successful friend and they work ridiculous hours, click on Deliveroo in the evening, they have maybe half an hour of [a] gym session in a week, which can be quite harmful. They’re not moving all day, they’re not sleeping, and they’re probably eating and drinking rubbish,” he says. The answer is not more “wellness”, he argues, but kind of the opposite – fewer products, fewer interventions, fewer things being sold to us as solutions. “You need less,” he says. “And actually, that doesn’t cost anything, and I’m not making any profit in telling you that.” Personally, I just can’t see it catching on.
summary: Private GP Christian Collins argues that modern society's culture of abundance and perpetual consumption is the root cause of poor health. Rather than adopting extreme biohacking or buying wellness products, he advocates for moderation, lifestyle changes, and doing less. He notes that true wellbeing relies on fundamental aspects like sleep, exercise, and human connection rather than purchasing solutions.
key_points: Christian Collins reversed his own type 2 diabetes through diet, sleep, mindset, and exercise rather than relying on lifetime medication.
Conventional medicine focuses heavily on treating symptoms and keeping patients alive rather than prioritizing prevention or how a patient feels.
Collins suggests that safe, unproven remedies like magnesium supplements can still be useful if they help patients without causing harm.
A culture organized around perpetual consumption is fundamentally at odds with sustainable wellbeing.
The core solution to modern unhealthiness is often doing less and reducing consumption rather than buying more wellness products.

title: ‘Bored’ mother joined study – and found out her sons could have rare condition
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Revan Barker-Roe (left) and his brother Thorin](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498905303_17872443131070_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-vWbf2D_ysDrK1CwyHFV8UTb6FezYc_zyJm_l7jMDSw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Revan Barker-Roe (left) and his brother Thorin](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498905303_17872443131070_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq-vWbf2D_ysDrK1CwyHFV8UTb6FezYc_zyJm_l7jMDSw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A mother discovered her sons had a genetic change linked to a rare condition after signing up for a study because she was “bored”.
Jessica Barker-Roe, 32, found out her sons Revan and Thorin had a gene variant associated with adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), a progressive condition that affects the nervous system and adrenal glands.
Mrs Barker-Roe said the variant was detected only after she signed up for a research study screening 100,000 newborn babies in England for dozens of genetic conditions.
Most children are only diagnosed with ALD when symptoms appear and treatment options have become limited.
But after being found to have the gene variant, Revan and Thorin are being monitored closely by doctors, who will intervene early if symptoms appear.
Mrs Barker-Roe, from Bradford, West Yorkshire, said she first heard about the Generation Study, led by Genomics England in partnership with NHS England, during a long stay in hospital while pregnant with Revan, who is now eight months old.
![Brothers Revan (front) and Thorin Barker-Roe](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498905359_17872443320650_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqPjDZOdMgceQ0ik-fUDgEdk1yvS5SHwE7jkzuwNtqojw.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“The research midwives were just making their way around and chatting to patients, they asked me if I would be interested in signing up to the Generation Study,” she said.
“Honestly I was just bored so I said, ‘Yeah, whatever’ and put it to the back of my mind.”
The test involved a heel prick on Revan, revealing he had the genetic change associated with ALD – a condition which causes problems with vision, movement and understanding as well as adrenal problems.
Doctors also tested Revan’s brother, Thorin, now 4, which revealed he also has the gene change.
