“That happened really quickly because symptoms start around four years old, and once symptoms start it is really hard to treat it,” Mrs Barker-Roe said.
Boys to have MRI scans and blood tests
While having the genetic change does not necessarily lead to ALD, it does mean the boys can be monitored because treatment for neurological symptoms associated with ALD is only possible before symptoms start.
It is also important to treat adrenal symptoms early, therefore the boys will have MRI scans every six months until they are around 12 years old and blood tests to assess their adrenal glands.
Mrs Barker-Roe added: “I feel so lucky, instead of feeling worried, I feel so ridiculously lucky that we timed having a baby when the Generation Study was out there as an option and I was in hospital at a time when it was being offered by the research midwives because I had not heard of it.”
Her husband, Dominic Barker-Roe, 36, added: “We are now in a position where it’s surveillance and, if it does occur, the worst thing that could happen is surgery and a bone marrow transplant – yes, it comes with risk, but it is far less risky than the alternative.”
![The Barker-Roes](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498905306_17872443565920_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqd0IyrJnUAAY4-RjrvNT6cCBBHPDIdKsE2yvdzk778mY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Whole genome sequencing provides a readout of a person’s entire genetic code and looks for changes that relate to specific health conditions.
The Generation Study, which was launched in 2024, screens for these conditions in babies who appear healthy but whose symptoms may not become apparent until later in life.
The research project is available at more than 70 hospitals in England and will help identify more than 200 rare conditions.
The study will generate evidence on whether and how whole genome sequencing should be offered to every baby as part of screening for rare genetic conditions at birth, alongside the existing heel prick test – which looks for 10 rare but serious conditions.
So far, more than 85,000 families have joined the study and more than 200 “condition suspected” results have been returned by Genomics England to the NHS for confirmatory testing.
‘Early detection gives family best start’
Prof Richard Scott, the chief executive at Genomics England, said: “We are really pleased that the Generation Study has helped Revan’s family receive an early result for both of their children.
“This is exactly the kind of evidence the study is designed to build, showing how whole genome sequencing at birth could support earlier diagnosis, earlier care and better understanding of rare genetic conditions.”
Dr Catriona Firth, a consultant neonatologist at Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, said: “Early detection has given Revan and his family the best possible start.
“Identifying this genetic change meant we were able to refer to the specialists in this rare condition straight away. Through discussion with the experts the family have been made aware of the implications of the test result.
“Signs and symptoms of ALD are non-specific, so the disorder usually takes time to diagnose even after concerns arise. The Generation Study test result means both boys can be monitored, so if there are signs of change, treatment can be started straight away.”
Prof Dame Sue Hill, chief scientific officer at NHS England, said: “By bringing genomic research and routine NHS care together, we can help families get answers sooner while building the evidence for how genomics could improve newborn care in the future.”
summary: A mother who joined a newborn genetic study out of boredom discovered that her infant son and older brother carry a gene variant linked to adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD). The rare, progressive condition typically goes undiagnosed until symptoms appear and treatment options become limited. Because of the early detection through the Generation Study, both boys are now being closely monitored by doctors with regular MRIs and blood tests to intervene early if necessary.
key_points: Jessica Barker-Roe signed up for the Generation Study while pregnant after being approached by research midwives in the hospital.
A heel-prick test on her infant son Revan revealed a gene variant associated with ALD, prompting tests that showed his four-year-old brother Thorin also has the variant.
ALD affects the nervous system and adrenal glands, usually only being diagnosed after symptoms start and treatment becomes difficult.
The boys will now undergo regular monitoring, including MRI scans every six months, allowing doctors to provide early interventions before symptoms develop.
The Generation Study, led by Genomics England and NHS England, aims to screen 100,000 newborn babies for dozens of rare genetic conditions.

title: 'It's a bit odd at first': The robot helping with NHS health checks
author: Lisa Summers
content:
![A man seated in a clinic or office consultation room using a digital health monitoring device. A blood pressure cuff is attached to one arm, with the device resting on a desk. A touchscreen unit stands nearby, and computer monitors are visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/2578/live/111341e0-9ce3-11f1-9e72-05a4f32fdb83.jpg)
Ged Cashley has annual checks to monitor his health
- Published
Ged Cashley suffered a cardiac arrest in 2018 and now has annual checks to monitor his health.
The 72-year-old's latest trip to the doctor was a little different to his previous ones.
His GP practice in Dundee is trialling a 3ft-tall robot - called Teme - which glides across the waiting room and takes him through a series of checks before he sees the doctor.
"It's a bit odd at first, but you soon get used to it," says Ged.
âThe first part of almost every patient consultation is spent collecting basic information.
"The little robot does that job - so by the time you sit down with your GP, they already have what they need and can spend their time actually talking to you.â
Robot carries out health check on patient
Ged's GP - Dr Gillian Chin - believes robots could play a key role in freeing up healthcare staff to see "more patients, more quickly".
Her surgery took part in a two-day trial called HEART-POD, a collaboration with scientists at the National Robotarium at Heriot Watt University, who developed a prototype robot.
In total, 12 patients living with cardiovascular conditions took part.
For the trial, the robot carried out basic checks such as blood pressure monitoring, oxygen saturation as well as weight measurements.
The robot, which currently has an American accent, greets the patient in the waiting room and takes them to an examination room where it talks them through tasks such as how to unwrap the blood pressure cup, place their arm flat on the table and start the monitor.
Teme then speaks to the patients before printing out the results so they can be taken to the nurse or GP for further discussion.
![Dr Gillian Chin is wearing a checked yellow shirt and headband.  She is in her GP surgery  - Erskine Medical Practice in Dundee](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/1f09/live/5ba7d530-9cb7-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Dr Gillian Chin is a GP at Erskine Medical Practice in Dundee
"It's undeniable that the NHS is under pressure," Dr Chin told BBC Scotland News.
"Demand on the system is increasing at a higher rate than the number of appointments and capacity that we're able to offer."
She said using the robot saved 50% of consultation time, allowing a doctor or nurse to either see more patients or go into greater detail with them.
According to Dr Chin, feedback was largely positive from staff and patients but it identified issues that would need to be addressed ahead of wider deployment.
Some patients in the trial expressed concerns about privacy, preferring not to talk to the robot in the waiting room.
![Ged Cashley is wearing a blue shirt and glasses.  The 72 year old suffered a cardiac arrest in 2018 and now has annual health checks.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c497/live/653beb90-9cb7-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Ged Cashley has annual health checks after having a cardiac arrest in 2018
The use of robots in the NHS is not an entirely new area.
Robotic assisted surgery has already been welcomed by surgeons who say it allows them to perform complex operations with faster recovery for patients.
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools have also been used successfully in some parts of the NHS, such as helping radiologists detect cancer.
However, the use of AI and robots has also prompted concern about diagnostic accuracy, patient confidentiality and workforce levels.
![A robotic engineer is working with a prototype of a humanoid robot in a large laboratory at Heriot Watt University](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/3b32/live/88b03b80-9596-11f1-863d-591d6d16ad3c.jpg)
The National Robotarium at Heriot Watt University
The Royal College of GPs Scotland believe robots performing simple tasks can have an important role in supporting doctors.
But its vice chair Dr Chris Williams said: "Technology should be seen as a tool to support healthcare professionals, not replace them.
"The human relationship between patients and clinicians cannot be replicated by technology alone."
Colin Poolman, executive director of the RCN in Scotland, said âNursing staff welcome investment in solutions that support them to be more effective in their roles."
But he also said there had to be a balance.
"Technology is a support for nursing staff, not a substitute,â he said.
![Lisa Farrell is wearing a green top and jacket and stands beside a humanoid robot at the National Robotarium](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b3e3/live/8942a330-9cb7-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Lisa Farrell is the business development lead for healthcare robotics
Those involved in developing robotic technology believe it could be moving at a faster pace and used more widely.
"We're seeing really quick developments in terms of humanoid robots that can help, perhaps, around the home, in our leisure and retail centres," said Lisa Farrell, business development lead for Healthcare Robotics at The National Robotarium.
"What we're not seeing at the moment is that uptake in our health services."
Farrell says healthcare robots are not designed to take jobs away from professionals but could be used to do some of the "dull, dirty or dangerous" tasks to free people up "to do what humans do best".
She said countries like the US and Japan are further ahead in the adoption of healthcare robots but says here in Scotland and the UK it needs "momentum and political will now".
'No national strategy' for robots
The National Robotarium is involved in several small scale pilots like the one in Dundee.
The centre also piloted healthcare robots in a hospital in Paris, external and is soon to carry out a test in a care home in Glasgow. Most are currently funded by private companies.
Professor of economics and project co-investigator Cristina Tealdi said the technology is improving at a fast pace and is adaptable to need.
What is missing, she said, is national investment and testing in real life situations to collect data on what offers best value to the NHS and patients.
"At the moment the implementation is very scattered and there is not a national strategy towards implementation of technology in healthcare," she said.
Health Secretary Angela Constance said innovation within the health and care system was central to plans for reform.
She said the government had already taken "significant measures" to use technology, including âsupporting AI-powered physiotherapy services and a Â£1.8m investment in a national digital dermatology platform, now available to all GPs to cut waiting times and support earlier skin cancer diagnosis".
summary: A GP practice in Dundee recently trialled a 3ft-tall robot named Teme to help conduct basic patient health checks and gather initial information. Developed in collaboration with the National Robotarium, the trial aimed to see if technology could save consultation time and alleviate NHS pressures. While the initial test showed that the robot saved 50% of consultation time and received generally positive feedback, it also highlighted privacy concerns and the need for a balanced approach that supports rather than replaces healthcare professionals.
key_points: A Dundee GP surgery trialled a prototype robot named Teme to perform basic health checks like measuring blood pressure and weight.
The trial found that using the robot saved 50% of consultation time, helping free up doctors and nurses.
Some patients expressed privacy concerns about interacting with the robot in the waiting room.
Medical organizations emphasize that technology should act as a support tool for staff rather than a replacement for human clinicians.
Experts note that while technology is advancing quickly, the NHS lacks a unified national strategy for implementing healthcare robotics.

title: A split in the spectrum? The ongoing battle to define autism
author: Catherine Burns
content:
![Catherine Burns](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/b00a/live/3312d620-9ca7-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
If someone asked you to think of an autistic person, who would come to mind?
The world's richest man, Elon Musk?
Maybe Greta Thunberg, who says being different can be a superpower.
Or Robbie Williams, who has recently revealed he's found out that he has "a bit of autism".
What about someone like 34-year old James Fitzpatrick? He doesn't talk, has a learning disability and needs constant care.
A diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) means someone has certain core characteristics including differences in how they communicate and behave. It's an umbrella term that includes people with very different experiences.
In recent years there has been an explosion in the number of people with an autism diagnosis on their GP record. In England, it has gone from just over 700,000 three years ago to around 1.1 million today.
The National Autistic Society (NAS) says "evidence suggests there is a significant underdiagnosis of autism, particularly among women and older people".
But what if some people with a diagnosis aren't actually autistic? What if they've really been misdiagnosed?
These questions largely come from 85-year-old Professor Dame Uta Frith - one of the key figures in autism research since the 1960s.
They go to the heart of a debate that is central to the identity of many autistic people.
![Greta Thunberg wearing a white t-shirt and patterned scarf. She is photographed while talking](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/7225/live/3c585750-9ca7-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Greta Thunberg says her autism is a superpower
Dame Uta says this is about misdiagnosis - people wrongly being told they are autistic.
She is reluctant to say how many people she thinks have wrongly told they have autism: "In my worst moments, I think it's a great number, but in my best moments, I think it is a small number."
Dame Uta is worried that autistic people who need a lot of support are not getting the help they need.
Some autism researchers and charities say her views are "dangerous", "misinformation" and pit "autistic people against each other". Many autistic people are angry too, saying this calls their identity and rights into question.
The increase in diagnoses of neurodivergent conditions such as autism and ADHD, along with a steep rise in people reporting poor mental health, has prompted a government-commissioned independent review that is due to be published shortly.
But whatever its findings, it is unlikely to be the final word on a question that affects so many people: what actually is autism? And does it matter if such a broad spectrum of people are defined as having it?
Shifting meanings
The definition of autism has shifted and evolved since it was coined in 1911. Then, it was described as a symptom of childhood schizophrenia - excessive fantasies and hallucinations.
By 1943, autism was used to describe children with "fascinating peculiarities" who weren't interested in the world around them.
In the 1960s, it was estimated that 0.04% of children were autistic and most had intellectual disabilities.
By the early 1980s, researchers embraced the idea of an autism spectrum, arguing that autistic people could have average - or very high - intelligence.
This new category of autism was known as Asperger's Syndrome after a little-known paper dating back to Austria in the 1940s, but the term is no longer used.
In 2013, ASD became the official diagnosis for all autistic people. But some autism experts think this is too broad.
Dame Uta ignited this debate by arguing that the autistic spectrum has come to its collapse because people included in it have such different needs.
Questioning the spectrum
A quick search through social media tells you that the 85-year-old is "a pioneer", "brilliant" and the "grand dame of autism research".
But also, a "traitor", an "out-of-touch grifter" who is "past her sell-by date".
During one of our conversations, she receives an email - hate mail. It tells her she will have blood on her hands and contains expletives.
She says: "Some people would say it would be better for me to stop. But I want to get at the truth."
But, even so, she hesitated for years before speaking out, partly because she "really, really" doesn't want to hurt people.
She talks about being driven by "almost a duty" to represent autistic people with intellectual disabilities. She thinks they are being ignored "both in research and in general awareness".
About a third of autistic people have intellectual disabilities. But they are underrepresented in research - a 2019 study found that they make up about 6% of research participants.
Dame Uta says: "These cases are in great need of support. They have been completely overshadowed."
She would include this group on a "pruned" autism spectrum along with people who have what used to be known as Asperger's and autistic people who are diagnosed during childhood.
![Hans Asperger standing up at a conference. He wears a light suit and is surrounded by other delegates. The photograph is black and white](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9ead/live/48c8b2a0-9ca7-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
The term Asperger's was named for the psychiatrist Hans Asperger, but the term has since been dropped
She thinks the rise in autism diagnoses is driven by a "late-diagnosed group, mainly females".
The NHS says it can be difficult to recognise autism in women, but Dame Uta says: "I am sceptical of late diagnosis. That's where I think the diagnostic process has become very superficial."
She believes many of this group actually have other conditions including anxiety, depression or OCD.
She questions: "Are they best served by this label autism? I would like them to get better service than they're getting."
She also thinks researchers might need to create "a label that doesn't exist yet" for some people who've been told they're autistic.
She points to research from the University of Cambridge which found that people diagnosed with autism in early childhood often have a different genetic profile to people diagnosed when they are older. Researchers found that people diagnosed when they are older (from late childhood onwards) show an underlying genetic profile that has more in common with ADHD and depression than it does with early diagnosed autism.
But the lead researcher, Dr Varun Warrier, says this shows "autism broadening out genetically" rather than misdiagnosis.
Dame Uta thinks a small number don't have any mental health conditions at all - but are "identity seekers" who have been influenced by bad information on social media.
She hasn't got a number for how many people she thinks have been misdiagnosed, but believes researchers could figure it out.
She knows this will upset and possibly scare people. She stresses: "If someone has been misdiagnosed, I don't want them to suffer for it.
"It would be a terrible thing to take away a diagnosis retrospectively. It's the future I'm concerned with, making diagnostic process more precise - targeting very different individual needs rather than a label."
Culture wars
Dame Uta first expressed her views in an interview with the Times Educational Supplement in March. The NAS reacted to it in strong terms.
It wrote a blog post about "false narratives and outdated ideas", "misinformation" and "false claims".
Dame Uta says it's "just wrong" to dismiss her like this.
The NAS says anyone with an autism diagnosis will have been assessed against strict criteria and "have lifelong differences in communication, behaviours and focused interests compared to non-autistic people".
Dr Sue Smith, the NAS's head of clinical services, says: "We've got a group of people with a genuine need. We're having this weird debate about what they should be called."
She says this isn't just an academic row but has real implications for autistic people: "Historically a lot of people who weren't properly identified as autistic were given other really unhelpful labels", such as borderline personality disorder or bipolar.
She worries that re-labelling some autistic people could lead to them losing support.
Dr Monique Botha, an associate professor of psychology at Durham University, criticised Dame Uta's opinion using swear words.
Botha is autistic and stands by her reaction: "A lot of people were understandably upset and angryâ¦ I still am.
"Researchers have a duty to be a bit more blunt and upfront about how damaging these kinds of things can be."
Botha feels that Dame Uta's ideas add to a narrative that "there's some magical easy autism where you're just quirky, where everything in your life will eventually work out, and you're just using this as a crutch so that you can feel special, and it trivialises the reality of a whole bunch of people".
Botha says autistic people are united by key features: sensory sensitivity, a need for predictability, intense interests and struggles with communication.
"That doesn't mean that we will have the same lives or the same outcomes."
James Fitzpatrick was diagnosed in the 1990s, and doesn't speak. His father, Dr Michael Fitzpatrick, is a retired GP.
![Michael and James Fitzpatrick sit on a sofa together. Michael wears a grey shirt and dark trousers, and james wears a red Batman t-shirt and dark tracksuit bottoms](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0389/live/5c3dc6e0-9ca7-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Michael's son, James, has very high care needs
Michael says he's been shocked by the response to Dame Uta's stance: "Intolerant, strident, abusive discourse that's very redolent of the culture wars."
He feels some autistic people don't understand the reality for his family.
Michael says that James, now 34, has "never developed the capacity to engage with the world. That's the source of profound sadness to his family and a loss to himself."
"He would injure himself, bang his head on the floor, bite himself. If you tried to stop him, he would also bite you or scratch you or headbutt you. And as he got bigger, that became more of a problem."
James has calmed down with age but still can "attack you randomly for no apparent reason".
Michael can't see how the same diagnosis can hold true for James and for someone who lives independently - two "extremely different types of people".
Different challenges
Dr Rachel Moseley, an academic from Bournemouth University, was working in autism research when she was diagnosed in her late 20s.
She agrees that people like James are "incredibly neglected".
But she says: "There's room for all of us, we can still advocate for people with learning disabilities without saying that this group isn't valid."
She thinks ideas about dividing up the autistic spectrum lack nuance, especially around mental health.
"Every so often something will totally knock my feet out from under me," Moseley adds, saying she will self-harm and have suicidal thoughts.
"Everyone's challenges are different. But you can't make the assumption that the person with high support needs is always having a harder time. They will in some regards, but not in all."
To make her point, she cites studies that have found that while autistic people overall are more likely to take their own lives, these rates are highest in autistic people without learning disabilities.
Michael Fitzpatrick is unconvinced by this argument: "I seriously, seriously doubt whether the people with autism and no levels of learning disability have a similar level of pathology and life-threatening problems as the people with profound autism."
Lived experience
It's striking that both sides in this row accuse the other of lacking scientific rigour. One major flashpoint is around the study of masking.
This is when someone hides autistic behaviours to try to fit in with society. There's been an explosion of academic interest in this area.
Recently, a review found almost 400 research papers talking about masking, mostly focusing on autistic women who were diagnosed as adults and don't have any intellectual disabilities.
Dame Uta shudders when I mention the idea: "Agh! Such a vague notion." She dismisses some research papers on it as "absolutely poor quality".
Moseley says the exact opposite: "There is really high-quality work on masking, and it's startling and upsetting to see such work be denigrated."
She sees masking research as part of a "refreshing change" as autistic academics "bring lived experience into research".
But Dame Uta questions if autistic researchers can be neutral or if they have a conflict of interest.
![Professor Dame Uta Frith standing in front of a river. She has short grey hair, glasses, pearls and is wearing a dark coat](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6033/live/c0aa81a0-9ca6-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Dame Uta ignited the row earlier this year
She's something of an outlier with this view.
Professor Sir Simon Baron-Cohen is director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge. When he started out, Dame Uta was his mentor. He disagrees with her on this.
He says: "Someone who's got a degree in molecular biology has one kind of expertise, but someone who's got lived experience has got another kind."
Overall though, Sir Simon says: "I'm not taking sides. I think the answer is to get both sides round the table. A lot of what seem to be irreconcilable differences are actually reconcilable."
He does think the term autism is too broad and can lead to "lumping together people who are so different".
His suggestion is to add sub groups. Type one could be autism with a learning disability. Type two could be autism with language needs. Other types could include conditions that can co-occur with autism, such as ADHD, depression and epilepsy.
He says: "Imagine, we could have dozens or hundreds of subtypes. Why put a limit on it? The more we have, the more precise we can be about what people need."
Once again, there is no consensus.
Dame Uta thinks subtypes could provide "a clean division between those who have these very severe needs and those who don't. But it can't go on endlessly."
The NAS is worried that breaking autism into smaller groups could lead to discrimination or the removal of support from people who need it. It says subtypes have "no clinical value, diagnostic relevance or practical application".
Sir Simon's answer is to "bring in autistic people so we can choose labels that they're comfortable with".
Moving goalposts
Kayleigh was diagnosed with autism in her thirties. She finds that people hold pre-conceived ideas about what autism is.
She explains: "Some will assume you can't spell your own name. Or you love trains. Or you're extremely clever. Or you're hyper focused on a boring hobby."
Since diagnosis she's been given various labels - Asperger's, high-functioning and AuDHD [Autistic with ADHD].
She says: "The goalposts keep moving. As an autistic person, I don't even know what I should be called."
For her, this row is a huge distraction from the real issues.
She's spent her life thinking she was "weird, sub-normal or really, really bad". She's angry that society didn't recognise that she was struggling.
Since diagnosis, she says she's had "zero" support from professionals. She says emotionally she feels she can only really go out if her family are with her. She's not been to her local town centre in years.
She wants more help, more understanding. She doesn't care what her condition is called.
She says: "You could call it 'silly brain disease'. I still know what I'm going through."
Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell

summary: Professor Dame Uta Frith has sparked an intense debate by arguing that the modern autism spectrum has become too broad and that many late-diagnosed individuals, particularly women, may be misdiagnosed. While some researchers and family members of individuals with high support needs support her concerns about the neglect of those with intellectual disabilities, critics argue her views are dangerous, dismissive, and threaten the identities and support systems of autistic people. The controversy highlights a deep ongoing division within the scientific and autistic communities regarding how autism is defined and diagnosed.
key_points: Professor Dame Uta Frith argues that the autism spectrum has collapsed under the weight of vastly different experiences, leading to potential misdiagnoses.
The number of autism diagnoses on GP records in England has risen significantly, from just over 700,000 three years ago to around 1.1 million.
Critics, including charities and autistic researchers, condemn Frith's views as misinformation and argue that narrowing the spectrum could strip vulnerable people of necessary support.
About a third of autistic people have intellectual disabilities, and supporters of Frith's view argue this group is severely underrepresented and overshadowed in research.

title: Devon farmer has vaccinated 1,700 sheep for bluetongue
author: Hattie McCann; Julia Gregory
content:
![Mark Walter is standing in front of a gated enclosure at a livestock market. 
He is wearing a red and white checked shirt and brown waistcoat.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/792f/live/2c01b490-9cbc-11f1-84cf-fd4cfd9d6c84.jpg)
Mark Walter has vaccinated hundreds of sheep in just a few days
- Published
A farmer has spoken about the impact of protecting livestock from the bluetongue virus which can make sheep and cattle lethargic and lame, it can cause birth defects or spontaneous abortions and it can be fatal.
Mark Walter, who farms in Milton Damerel in north Devon said bluetongue has caused "a lot of stress".
He said: "I've probably injected 400 plus sheep with antibiotics. We've vaccinated 1,700 sheep in total.
Devon has the highest number of places with the virus in England and Wales, with 304 premises where it has been detected, as of Wednesday, with 105 sites in Cornwall.
![Ele Brown is wearing a a sleeveless pale blue top. She has shoulder length blonde hair and is standing outside with several  sheds in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/dd6d/live/2c3b9e60-9cbe-11f1-a9cd-fd8bcb95d396.jpg)
Ele Brown said the virus thrives in hot conditions
He feared 40% of his lambs could be born stillborn or with disabilities because of bluetongue.
He added: "All we were doing is jabbing sheep day and night. The poor sheep, it was horrendous for them."
The government's deputy chief veterinary officer Ele Brown joined farmers for a meeting at Holsworthy Market in Devon on Thursday to discuss their concerns and give them an update on the virus.
The first cases of bluetongue in the UK for 15 years were recorded in 2023-24.
![A field of very dry brown short grass with a flock of more than 20 sheep.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/0be2/live/486485b0-9cbf-11f1-a9cd-fd8bcb95d396.png)
The virus can spread through infected pregnant animals transmitting it to their young
Brown said the number of cases were "particularly bad" in Devon and Cornwall because of the high number of cows and sheep and weather conditions being "perfect" for midges.
She added: "That really ramps up the amount of virus there is and unfortunately that means animals down here are picking up the infection."
The midges which carry bluetongue and the virus itself are "really temperature sensitive", she added.
"If the warm weather survives into the autumn midges will still be active, will still be feeding.
"If the average day and night temperatures stay at above 12C (53F) or 13C (55F) we'll still see virus replicating in them, so everything that pushes that heat really prolongs that period."
Vaccination
She said the government "spent a lot of of time" in 2024-25 "trying to stop the spread" once the virus arrived in the UK and has been trying to persuade farmers to get their stock vaccinated.
Brown added the uptake has been around 10% and "it just means that not enough animals have been protected and so unfortunately we're seeing that spike in disease signs".
NFU president for England and Wales Tom Bradshaw who was also at the meeting called for the government to compensate farmers for disposing of any "fallen stock".
He added: "We need that vaccine here as quickly as possible so it can be rolled out here and in other parts of the country where we know its spreading to very very quickly."
He said reporting of vaccination needs to be "more streamlined".
Currently farmers have to report vaccinating each individual animal, Bradshaw said.
Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.
summary: Devon farmer Mark Walter has vaccinated 1,700 sheep against the bluetongue virus, which causes lethargy, lameness, birth defects, and potential fatalities in livestock. Devon currently has the highest number of premises with the virus in England and Wales, with 304 detected sites. Government officials and farming representatives recently met in Devon to discuss the outbreak, low vaccine uptake, and the impact of warm weather on midge activity.
key_points: Farmer Mark Walter vaccinated 1,700 sheep and injected over 400 with antibiotics due to the bluetongue outbreak.
Devon leads England and Wales with 304 premises affected by the virus, alongside 105 sites in Cornwall.
The government's deputy chief veterinary officer stated that warm weather creates perfect conditions for the midges that spread the virus.
National Farmers' Union (NFU) president Tom Bradshaw called for government compensation for disposing of fallen stock and a more streamlined vaccination reporting process.

title: UK men with heart disease at higher risk of developing and dying from cancer
author: Andrew Gregory
content:
Millions of men with heart disease have a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer, according to a decades-long study.
The biggest drivers behind male cases were smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol, researchers said, with the link most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Analysing health data from 22,000 Britons over 25 years, researchers at the University of Aberdeen and Keele University discovered stark gender differences in outcomes of people living with heart disease.
About half the participants – 11,000 – had cardiovascular disease (CVD) at the start of the study, or developed it over the next three decades.
The lifetime risk of cancer among those with CVD was higher in men (17.3%) compared with women (12.8%), the study found. In those without CVD, cancer risk was 10.2% among men and 8.2% for women.
Dr Tiberiu Pana, a specialty registrar in cardiology at NHS Grampian and honorary early career clinical research fellow at the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that cancer incidence and death were higher in people with cardiovascular disease than in those without – a relationship we already knew a bit about.
“However, through looking at this large patient group over a very long period of time we were able to examine it more thoroughly. We have identified clear differences between men and women across a range of factors in those with cardiovascular disease and all types of cancer.”
Further analysis of cancers outside of the reproductive system suggested that people with heart disease faced higher rates of gastric, oesophageal, lung, bowel and non-melanoma skin cancers.
These were also more prominent among men, according to the study. The results were published in the European Heart Journal.
Men with CVD also had an increased risk of dying from gastric, oesophageal and lung cancers compared with those without heart disease. This may be driven by common risk factors between CVD and cancer, researchers said.
Mamas Mamas, a professor of cardiology at Keele University, said more research was needed to better understand the reasons behind the increased cancer risk in people with heart disease.
“Furthermore, whilst cardio-oncology services have focused mainly on cancer patients preventing the development of cardiovascular diseases, we need better pathways that can identify and prevent cancer development in patients with cardiac conditions.”
Nicola Smith, a senior health information manager at the charity Cancer Research UK, said: “Many causes of cancer and heart disease overlap, which may explain why there’s a link between the two, and both of these diseases are more common in people from deprived areas.”
Cancer is slightly more likely to affect men, partly because smoking rates are higher, Smith said, but more research was needed to confirm the stronger link between heart disease and cancer in men compared to women.
“If anyone is concerned about their risk of cancer or heart disease, there are proven steps they can take to reduce it. These include not smoking, keeping a healthy weight, and cutting down on alcohol.”
summary: A 25-year study of 22,000 Britons by researchers at the University of Aberdeen and Keele University found that men with heart disease face a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer compared to women with heart disease and individuals without heart conditions. The primary drivers identified for male cancer cases were smoking, obesity, and excessive alcohol consumption. The findings, published in the European Heart Journal, highlight the need for better healthcare pathways to identify and prevent cancer in patients with cardiac conditions.
key_points: Men with cardiovascular disease had a 17.3% lifetime risk of cancer, compared to 12.8% for women with CVD.
The strongest cancer links in men with heart disease were found in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Smoking, obesity, and drinking too much alcohol were identified as the biggest drivers behind male cancer cases.
Researchers suggest that common risk factors between cardiovascular disease and cancer may explain the link between the two.

title: In the hills of northeast India, villagers grow living bridges by guiding the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers for 15 to 30 years — and unlike any bridge built by human hands, the older these get, the stronger they become
author: Space Daily; Ainura Kalau
content:
A living root bridge starts out looking like something somebody forgot to pull up. A single pale root, no thicker than a shoelace, gets threaded by hand through a hollowed-out betel nut trunk laid across a stream.
Come back in twenty or thirty years and that same root has thickened, spread, and fused with a dozen others into a structure solid enough for a small crowd to cross at once. Most things humans build get weaker with age. This is the rare one that does the opposite.
The structures are called jingkieng jri by the Khasi and Jaintia communities who grow them, across the hills of Meghalaya in northeast India. The name translates roughly to root bridge, which undersells what’s actually happening. Nobody is building these the way we usually mean that word. They’re growing them, on a timeline that outlasts the person who starts one.
The bridge that starts as a single root and a hollow trunk
The process begins with planting a Ficus elastica, the rubber fig, on the bank of a river or the edge of a ravine. Once the tree is established and starts sending out aerial roots, someone guides the young, flexible roots horizontally rather than letting them drop straight down, threading them through hollowed betel nut trunks or lengths of bamboo laid across the gap like a temporary scaffold. The roots grow along that guide until they reach the far side and anchor there.
Meghalaya’s biodiversity board puts the timeline at fifteen to twenty-five years before a bridge can safely carry a person’s weight, next to three or four years for a comparable concrete span. Once it’s there, a finished bridge can reportedly hold up to fifty people crossing at once. Gaps between roots eventually get packed with stones for an even walking surface, and some bridges get handrails woven in too.
“We call it meiramew, which means ‘the profound act of giving and merging with mother nature,'” says Montila Khongbeh, a resident of Mawkyrnot village. Building one is a multi-generation commitment, and the matrilineal Khasi communities that grow these bridges treat it that way, with women reportedly doing much of the ongoing tending. The skill itself isn’t widely spread. Fewer than two dozen elders are thought to still hold the full building knowledge, passed down mostly during the rainy season, when young roots are pliable enough to weave.
Everything else we build is fighting a losing argument with time
An ordinary bridge starts losing ground the day it opens. Steel corrodes, concrete develops microfractures under repeated freeze and thaw, timber rots where water sits. Engineers can slow this with maintenance schedules, but they can’t reverse it, because the material itself is fixed the moment it’s poured or welded into place. A bridge is at its structural best on day one.
A living root bridge does the reverse, because the material never stopped being alive. “Stable bridges like these made of closely intertwined roots can reach more than 50 meters in length and exist for several hundreds of years,” says Ferdinand Ludwig, professor of green technologies in landscape architecture at the Technical University of Munich, who has documented dozens of these structures directly.
We came across a video a while back that gets into part of this story in more depth than an article really can. It walks through the idea that a root tip isn’t just growing blindly toward water and nutrients. It behaves something like a sensing organ, picking up gravity, moisture, and chemical signals in the soil and adjusting course accordingly, sending faint electrical pulses through the ground the whole way, with no central brain coordinating any of it. Watching it laid out made the Meghalaya bridges make a different kind of sense to us. The roots aren’t following a blueprint someone drew up once. They’re responding, over and over, for decades, to exactly the load a person is asking them to carry.
His colleague on the same research, Thomas Speck, professor of botany at the University of Freiburg, explains the mechanism in plainer terms: “The roots react to mechanical loads with secondary root growth.” Put simply, the parts of a root doing the most work get measurably thicker over time, in direct response to the job they’re being asked to do.
What the roots are actually doing while nobody’s watching
What are the roots actually doing, mechanically, while they thicken and reach for each other? A 2019 survey published in Scientific Reports mapped 76 living root bridges across three expeditions between 2015 and 2017, geolocating 72 of them. Spans ranged from 2 to 52.7 meters, at elevations from just above sea level up past 1,200 meters, and roughly 80 percent came in under 20 meters long. The same researchers compared the cross-sections of roots that had spent years carrying a horizontal load against roots simply growing straight down under their own weight. The vertical roots stayed mostly round. The horizontal, load-bearing ones flattened and elongated into something closer to a T-shape, the same basic move a structural engineer makes when adding material to the underside of a beam under bending load.
The researchers also documented how separate roots stop being separate. When two roots are pressed together at a crossing point long enough, they fuse through a process called inosculation, essentially the same wound-healing response a tree uses to close over an injury. A lattice that started as dozens of individual roots, each carrying its own share of the load, slowly becomes one continuous, load-sharing structure. That’s the actual, physical reason age works backward here: the extra years mean measurably more of the bridge has fused into a single, continuous piece.
A skill that might not outlive the bridges it built
In 2022, Meghalaya’s living root bridges were added to UNESCO’s tentative list for World Heritage status, a step toward the kind of formal recognition that tends to bring funding and attention with it. Architects and researchers, Ludwig among them, already treat building with living plants as a genuine option for future cities. That interest is arriving at an odd moment, though. The number of people who can actually grow one of these bridges from scratch is small and getting smaller, and most of what they know has never been written down anywhere at all.
A thirty-year-old root bridge in Meghalaya is nowhere near finished growing. Left alone, it keeps thickening, keeps fusing, keeps answering whatever load it’s asked to carry, for longer than most of the people who visit it will be alive. Whether the knowledge required to start the next one survives that long is a separate question, and right now nobody has a satisfying answer to it.
summary: In the hills of Meghalaya, India, the Khasi and Jaintia communities grow living root bridges by guiding rubber fig tree roots across streams over a period of 15 to 30 years. Unlike human-made structures that degrade over time, these bridges grow stronger with age as the intertwined roots thicken in response to mechanical loads and fuse together. While these sustainable bridges can last for hundreds of years and are being studied by modern architects, the traditional knowledge required to grow them is held by a dwindling number of elders.
key_points: Living root bridges are grown using the aerial roots of the rubber fig tree, guided across rivers using bamboo or betel nut trunks.
The process takes 15 to 30 years before a bridge can safely support human weight, and mature structures can hold up to 50 people at once.
Roots under mechanical load thicken over time and fuse together through inosculation, making the structures increasingly strong as they age.
The traditional building knowledge is a multi-generational commitment mostly held by fewer than two dozen elders in the matrilineal Khasi communities.
Meghalaya's living root bridges were added to UNESCO's tentative list for World Heritage status in 2022.

title: Why long gaps between meals may not be healthy for older people – new study
author: Adrián Carballo Casla
content:
Going for much of the day without eating is often promoted as a way to improve health or lose weight. But a new study suggests that long gaps between meals may have different effects on older adults – especially those in the oldest age groups.
For the study, my colleagues and I followed nearly 3,000 people aged 60 and over in Sweden and found that those who usually went longest without eating developed chronic diseases faster than those who had shorter gaps between meals. The difference was clearest among people aged 78 and over.
This does not mean that fasting causes disease in old age, nor that every older person should avoid long intervals without food. But it does raise questions about whether advice based on studies of younger and middle-aged adults can be safely applied to older age groups.
Fasting helps the body switch from using readily available sugar to using stored energy, such as fat. Studies in younger adults have linked some forms of fasting to better control of blood sugar and other potentially beneficial changes in metabolism. A recent review found that intermittent fasting led to modest weight loss and some improvements in metabolic health compared with eating without restrictions.
Older bodies, however, work differently in important ways. Ageing changes how people digest food, absorb nutrients, control blood sugar and maintain muscle. Older adults are also more likely to live with several long-term health conditions and take multiple medications. All these factors could change how fasting affects health.
Our study used data from 2,981 adults aged 60 and over who took part in a long-running Swedish study of ageing. When the study began between 2001 and 2004, participants were 74 years old, on average.
Participants reported their usual times for eating meals, snacks and drinking. We calculated the longest gap between any two times they ate or drank during a typical 24-hour day. This gave us a measure of their usual fasting time, rather than whether they followed a particular fasting diet.
We did not know whether people deliberately limited the hours in which they ate or simply went for long periods without food because of their appetite, health, personal preferences or other circumstances. Our analysis, though, took several of these factors into account.
![Swedes sitting outside in the snow.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/754833/original/file-20260819-50-idy283.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)
We then tracked diagnoses of 60 chronic diseases for up to 15 years. The diagnoses came from several sources, including in-person medical examinations, health histories, medication use, and patient registers. This allowed us to examine not only how many conditions people had, but how quickly that number increased.
Participants were divided into four groups, based on how long they typically went without eating each day. The shortest-fasting group went between six and 11.5 hours, while those in the longest-fasting group habitually did so for between 14 and 24 hours.
People who went 14 to 24 hours without eating developed chronic diseases faster than those with shorter fasting periods. This included cardiovascular diseases, such as heart failure and stroke, and neuropsychiatric conditions, such as depression and dementia. But it made no difference for musculoskeletal conditions like arthritis and osteoporosis.
Age appeared to matter. Among participants aged 78 and over, longer fasting was associated with faster accumulation of chronic diseases. We found no clear association among those aged 60 to 77.
Why age might change the picture
Several biological processes might explain why fasting has different effects at different ages. The digestive system can become less efficient in later life, reducing the absorption of essential nutrients such as vitamin B12, folate, calcium, and iron. Longer fasting compresses the time available for eating, potentially making it harder for older people to obtain and absorb enough nutrients.
Muscles also respond less effectively to protein with age. Eating protein regularly throughout the day provides repeated signals that help the body maintain muscle. Long gaps between meals may reduce these opportunities. Previous studies have linked muscle loss in older adults to ill health, including cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric diseases.
Medication use may also be important. Some medicines need to be taken with food to improve absorption or reduce side-effects, while others can affect blood sugar if taken far from meals. These explanations are plausible, but our study was not designed to identify the biological mechanisms behind the association of fasting with chronic conditions.
People who usually went longest without eating also tended to be older, eat fewer meals, consume less energy and protein, exercise less, and have more diseases when the study began. We took these and many other differences into account, including diet quality, smoking, sleep, education, living arrangements, social connections and care needs. The results were also similar when we repeated the analysis using different assumptions.
Even so, this was an observational study, so we cannot say that long fasting periods caused people to develop diseases faster. Poor health could instead lead people to skip meals, lose their appetite or change their eating habits. We took frailty and difficulties with everyday activities into account and still found similar results, but we cannot completely rule out the possibility that poor health caused the longer fasting periods rather than the other way around.
Participants were mainly highly educated, urban, community-dwelling older adults in Sweden. Eating patterns may differ in other countries, rural or disadvantaged communities, and among older people living in institutions. The meal-timing data were also collected more than two decades ago, and dietary habits may since have changed.
Taken together, these findings do not point to one ideal number of hours between meals. Instead, they suggest that fasting advice may need to account for age, nutritional vulnerability, medication use, and existing health problems. An eating pattern that offers some metabolic benefit earlier in adulthood may carry additional risks later in life, when getting enough nutrients, maintaining muscle and staying physically independent can become harder.
summary: A new study tracking nearly 3,000 adults aged 60 and over in Sweden found that those who maintained longer daily gaps between meals developed chronic diseases faster than those with shorter fasting periods. The difference was particularly clear among participants aged 78 and older, raising questions about whether fasting advice meant for younger adults is appropriate for older populations. Researchers suggest that age-related changes in digestion, nutrient absorption, muscle maintenance, and medication needs may explain why older bodies respond differently to long intervals without food.
key_points: Participants who went 14 to 24 hours without eating developed chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric conditions, faster than those with shorter fasting periods.
The association between longer fasting and the faster accumulation of chronic diseases was most evident among individuals aged 78 and over.
Long gaps between meals may make it harder for older adults to obtain sufficient nutrients and maintain muscle mass due to age-related physiological changes.
Because the research was an observational study, it cannot definitively prove that fasting causes disease faster, as pre-existing poor health could also lead to longer fasting times.

title: DR Congo to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine as Ebola infections surge
author: Anadolu; AP; Reuters
content:
![This photograph shows a vial of Ebola vaccine Ervebo in Freetown.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a87445e66e7-1787249758.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
As the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) struggles to manage its largest outbreak of the Ebola virus, it is set to receive 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine which has been effective in previous epidemics.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Thursday that the doses have been allocated from the global Ebola virus disease vaccine stockpile and would include 20,000 shots to be used in a late-stage trial to understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why is the latest Ebola outbreak worsening?
- list 2 of 4WHO: Ebola can be contained in months if enough funding is provided
- list 3 of 4DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak ‘global emergency’ as infections pass 5,000: WHO
- list 4 of 4How Ebola became the deadliest outbreak in DR Congo’s history
Bundibugyo is responsible for the current outbreak, which has so far killed 2,476 people out of the 5,208 confirmed cases.
The Ervebo vaccine is licensed for use against the Ebola virus – one of the viruses that cause Ebola disease – but not for Bundibugyo.
“It is not known whether Ervebo may be protective against the Bundibugyo virus in humans,” the WHO said, stressing the importance of clinical trials to provide new evidence.
To date, no vaccine or specific treatment has been approved for the Bundibugyo virus.
![Health workers stand in a new Ebola treatment center during a visit of Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), in Bunia, in the northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. \[May 31: AFP\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a874510dda1-1787249936.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Congolese government requested last week a release of Ervebo vaccines from the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision.
The remaining 50,000 shots will be used for front line and health workers, following recommendations from the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization, the WHO said.
The Geneva-based global vaccine alliance, Gavi, said it would provide $7m to fund the shipment to the DRC, along with another $6m to help with vaccination efforts in high-risk areas.
WHO Director-General, Tedros Ghebreyesus, said earlier this week that the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC remains a global emergency.
Stephane Dujarric, spokesman for the United Nations secretary-general, told reporters on Thursday that humanitarian agencies were warning of the continued spread of the outbreak as authorities seek to manage it.
“Our senior Ebola coordinator on the ground, Julian Harneis, said the government and our partners are scaling up the response with five operational priorities, including tripling safe care capacity, strengthening community engagement, doubling the number of safe and dignified burial teams and expanding disease surveillance and increasing support for the most vulnerable,” he said.
With support from the UN and its partners, the Congolese government also launched the “Congo River Without Ebola” initiative to intensify their response by strengthening disease surveillance and preparedness.
The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February.
summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is set to receive 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine to combat its largest Ebola outbreak, which has caused 5,208 confirmed cases and 2,476 deaths. Allocated from the global stockpile, 20,000 doses will fund a trial to test the vaccine against the Bundibugyo virus causing the outbreak, while 50,000 doses will protect frontline and health workers. Gavi is providing funding for the shipment and vaccination efforts, as the WHO continues to classify the outbreak as a global emergency.
key_points: DR Congo is receiving 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine from the global stockpile.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has resulted in 5,208 cases and 2,476 deaths.
No vaccine or specific treatment has been approved for the Bundibugyo virus, prompting a late-stage trial using 20,000 of the Ervebo doses.
Gavi is providing $7m for the shipment and $6m to support vaccination efforts in high-risk areas.
The WHO considers the eastern DR Congo Ebola outbreak to be a global emergency.

title: How going vegan for 1 month may affect aging, inflammation
author: Peter Morales-Brown
content:
![A lunchbox full of vegetables.](https://media.post.rvohealth.io/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/getty_2282929670_header_1296x728-1-1024x575.jpg)
- A recent study suggests that eating a vegan diet, even for a short time, may help reduce inflammation and slow biological aging.
- The diet aids in these areas by altering DNA methylation patterns, which are chemical markers that regulate gene expression.
- Although promising, the study findings are preliminary, and larger, longer-term studies are necessary to determine whether these changes could lead to meaningful health benefits.
Vegan dietary plans have gained popularity in recent years, with an increasing number of people opting to reduce or eliminate animal products from their diets. Concerns about animal welfare, the environmental impact of food production, and the potential health benefits likely influence this growing adoption.
As vegan options have become more widely available, following a vegan eating plan has also become more accessible and convenient. As a result, veganism has developed into a more mainstream dietary choice.
Now, a small randomized clinical trial suggests that eating a vegan diet for as little as 4 weeks may help reduce inflammation and even slow biological aging.
The findings, published in 
However, the study involved only 48 healthy adults, and lasted for a month. As such, larger, longer-term studies are needed to determine whether the changes persist and translate into better health outcomes.
Researchers from the University of California, San Diego, and the University of Freiburg analyzed blood samples from 48 healthy adults who first followed a standardized diet for a week. Participants were then randomly assigned to follow either a vegan diet or a meat-rich diet for a month.
The diets were designed to provide similar amounts of calories, allowing the researchers to investigate whether differences in food composition, rather than simply calorie intake or weight change, could account for the observed changes.
DNA methylation involves chemical modifications that do not alter underlying DNA, but can influence whether particular genes are more or less active. The researchers examined more than 800,000 DNA methylation sites across the genome before and after the dietary intervention.
They found several changes in the vegan group involving pathways related to immune function, metabolism, cell growth, insulin signaling, DNA repair, and cellular responses to stress.
As such, it suggests that adopting a vegan dietary plan may influence mechanisms that regulate gene activity.
“I find these findings interesting, but it is important we are careful with how we state the headline,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, RD, CDCES, CDN, a registered dietitian nutritionist who specializes in heart disease at EntirelyNourished, and who was not involved in this study.
“This study was a small, short term study in 48 healthy adults, and the researchers were looking at changes in DNA methylation, which is basically a chemical tagging system that helps control how genes are turned on and off. These changes can be influenced by diet, inflammation, activity, and aging. They are biological markers, not proof that someone is actually aging more slowly or will live longer.”
— Michelle Routhenstein, MS, RD
Similar previous research supports findings
“In 2023, we published the results of an 8-week study conducted in 22 pairs of identical twins. Our results were very similar to the recent study,” explained Christopher Gardner, PhD, the Rehnborg Farquhar Professor of Medicine at Stanford University, and Director of Nutrition Studies at the Stanford Prevention Research Center, who was also not involved in the study.
“We looked at chronological vs. biological aging with epigenetic clocks (similar to the recent study) and telomere length. In just 8 weeks, the twins randomized to these diets had aging measures that improved relative to their matched identical twins that were assigned a healthy omnivorous diet,” he continued.
Omnivores vs. vegans
“In our study, compared to the omnivorous study participants, the vegan participants experienced lower LDL-cholesterol, lower fasting insulin, lower weight, less aging (according to markers above), and had improved gut microbiome impacts.”
— Christopher Gardner, PhD
“We are not surprised by these recent findings, and are pleased to see that the types of findings we got in our study are being replicated in other studies. The replication makes the strength of the findings better solidified,” Gardner added.
The DNA methylation patterns in those following a vegan dietary plan were associated with lower proportions of neutrophils and higher proportions of CD4 T cells.
Neutrophils are white blood cells that play an important role in defending the body against infection. However, excessive or prolonged inflammatory activity can contribute to tissue damage and chronic disease. CD4+ T cells help coordinate and regulate immune responses against disease and infection.
The methylation-based estimates also correspond with blood-cell measurements obtained during the 
However, this does not mean that a vegan eating plan necessarily prevents inflammation or inflammatory disease.
Instead, the findings suggest that changing dietary patterns may influence biological pathways involved in the body’s immune response.
Unlike chronological age, which measures how many years a person has lived, biological age measures how the body is functioning. Researchers can estimate it using 
Two of the aging measures used in the study, PhenoAge and GrimAge, suggest that biological aging slowed in the vegan group during the 4-week intervention.
However, a third measure, Blood&Skin, produced a different result, showing age acceleration instead. This is important as different epigenetic clocks measure different aspects of aging and do not necessarily provide identical results.
Therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as a vegan eating plan reversing aging. Instead, they provide preliminary evidence that a short-term dietary intervention can affect molecular markers that researchers associate with biological aging.
The findings support the role of nutrigenomics, which is the study of how diet and genes interact to affect a person’s health and risk of developing diseases.
A well-planned vegan diet can provide substantial amounts of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds.
However, simply removing animal products does not automatically make a dietary plan healthy. A vegan diet can also include highly processed foods that are high in added sugars, sodium, or saturated fats, and may require a person to to pay attention to nutrients that can be more difficult to obtain from plant foods, including vitamin B12.
“It is important to recognize that when someone replaces a meat-heavy diet, they may also be eating less saturated fat and processed meat, which has been associated with aging,” Routhenstein told Medical News Today.
“I would not interpret these findings as meaning that animal foods are inherently inflammatory. It is more likely that the overall shift toward more plant foods and less processed and meat-heavy foods is influencing several pathways involved in inflammation and metabolism.”
“[T]he quality of the diet matters within a vegan diet. A diet can technically be vegan while being high in refined carbohydrates, sugary foods, fried foods, and highly processed vegan products,” Routhenstein said.
“[Y]ou do not have to go fully vegan to support healthy aging and longevity. Increasing the amount and variety of plant foods in your diet can provide many of these benefits while still allowing you to include animal foods,” she added.
“A good quality vegan diet is typically composed of foods and food groups that are recommended, and avoids or minimizes foods that are of low/lower nutritional quality,” Gardner told MNT.
“The recent study looked at inflammation and aging. However, there are decades of studies that suggest a good quality vegan diet is associated with lower risk of heart disease, cancer, diabetes, obesity and stroke, and their risk factors,” he said.
While encouraging, the study has several important limitations.
It was a small study that only included 48 healthy adults. As such, it may not be representative for how different people may respond to a vegan eating plan. Additionally, the intervention only lasted 4 weeks, so it is unclear whether the DNA methylation changes would remain after returning to usual diets, or whether maintaining a vegan diet for longer would produce larger or different effects.
Furthermore, the researchers only measure methylation changes in blood. Epigenetic patterns can differ between tissues, so changes in blood do not mean that identical changes may occur in organs such as the liver, brain, muscle, or adipose tissue.
The study also only measured molecular markers rather than long-term clinical outcomes. This means that it does not demonstrate that a vegan eating plan can prevent cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, or other age-related conditions, nor does it establish that the diet extends lifespan.
While further research is necessary, the findings suggest that the relationship between diet and health may extend beyond calories, body weight, and conventional blood markers, potentially reaching into the mechanisms that help regulate how cells function.
summary: A recent small, short-term clinical trial suggests that adopting a vegan diet for just four weeks can alter DNA methylation patterns, potentially reducing inflammation and slowing biological aging. However, experts emphasize that these findings are based on preliminary molecular markers rather than proof of extended lifespan or reduced disease. Larger and longer-term studies are needed to determine if these effects persist and translate into meaningful long-term health benefits.
key_points: A study of 48 healthy adults found that a four-week vegan diet altered DNA methylation patterns linked to immune function, metabolism, and cellular stress.
Two out of three aging measures suggested slowed biological aging in the vegan group, while a third measure showed age acceleration.
Experts caution that DNA methylation changes are biological markers and do not prove that a vegan diet reverses aging or prevents chronic disease.
The study's limitations include its small sample size, short four-week duration, and focus exclusively on blood tissue markers rather than long-term clinical outcomes.

title: Dr Amir Khan high cholesterol message to people on statins as thousands affected - AOL
author: Charlotte Smith
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Doctors office with a box of statin pills](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/20/34687b4a-b17c-337f-8841-83bae5620e63/97a82b4f-d89c-4780-b8a8-ec3989b3047e.jpg)
Dr Amir Khan has a message for anyone with high cholesterol, especially if they are taking statins and struggling. Speaking on the latest episode of his podcast, No Appointment Necessary, with co-host Cherry Healy, the NHS GP and ITV resident doctor discussed the common medical condition after a listener with high cholesterol sent in a question about being unable to tolerate statins.
Cherry read out the question: "Hi, I'm a 71-year-old female with a cholesterol level of eight. I can't tolerate any statins, having tried three different types. I'm worried sick. I will have a stroke or heart attack. Please, can you help me? I'm a non-smoker and a non-drinker."
Dr Amir Khan said that if a person has high total cholesterol levels, often above 7 or 7.5, it may indicate familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). It is a genetic condition in which the body produces high levels of cholesterol, and thousands are affected by it.
In the UK, it's estimated that between 220,000 and 270,000 people have FH, which means about one in every 250 people. Even though this condition is quite common, health organisations say that less than 10% of those with FH are officially diagnosed or recognised.
"So the first thing I would say is if you've got a total cholesterol above 7 or 7.5, there's probably a good chance you've got something called familial hypercholesterolemia", Dr Amir Khan said. "So that is where the genetics in your family make you produce high levels of cholesterol. So it's nothing you're doing, it is in your genes."
"Normally, for that, we would refer you to see a specialist in cholesterol, and they can talk you through the options. But there are still options your GP can prescribe for you. So I'm glad you've tried the statins. Don't try anymore. If you've tried three, that's that's enough. Statins are not for you."
Regarding statins, Dr Amir Khan advises that if a patient has already tried three different types without success or tolerability, they should not continue to try more. Instead, he suggests several alternatives, such as:
- Ezetimibe
- Bempedoic acid
- Inclisiran
Ezetimibe is an oral tablet that can be prescribed alongside statins or instead of them if statins are not tolerated. Bempedoic acid is another tablet option for those who may tolerate it better.
Inclisiran is an injectable treatment that can be administered sporadically. Dr Amir Khan says that these treatments are increasingly available directly through local GP surgeries rather than requiring a referral to a specialist lipid clinic.
![Female nurse drawing blood sample from woman in medical office](https://i2-prod.mirror.co.uk/incoming/article37572895.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_GettyImages-2097577382.jpg)
"Before these drugs, we had to refer to the lipid or cholesterol clinic," Dr Amir Khan said. "But now more and more of these things are coming into your GP surgery, and there are local GP surgeries working together to provide these services for their patients.
"So the best thing I would advise you to do is go and see your GP first of all, ask about this drug ezetimibe, which they can prescribe without any questions, and see if you respond to that. If not that, then it's bempedoic acid. If not that, then it's an inclisiran injection. There are lots of options available for you."
According to the NHS, FH is a genetic disease which results in the reduced clearance of atherogenic LDL-cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') in the blood, and an increased risk of early heart disease. It says: "People with FH have elevated LDL cholesterol levels from birth and children with FH show an increased thickness of their arteries compared to their non-FH siblings by the age of 11, showing the process of atherosclerosis development starts early in life.
"As a result of their FH, the incidence of fatal or non-fatal myocardial infarction without treatment is about 50% by the age of 50 years in men and about 30% by the age of 60 years in women."
The British Heart Foundation says that diagnosing FH begins with a routine blood lipid panel to evaluate LDL cholesterol levels. This is typically followed by specific DNA genetic testing, which can be conducted using a blood sample or a cheek swab. Doctors also assess physical signs and the family history of early heart disease, applying diagnostic criteria such as the Simon Broome or Dutch Lipid Clinic guidelines.
summary: NHS GP Dr Amir Khan addressed a listener's high cholesterol and inability to tolerate statins on his podcast, "No Appointment Necessary." He explained that total cholesterol levels above 7 or 7.5 often indicate familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), a genetic condition affecting thousands. Dr Khan advised stopping statins after three failed attempts and consulting a GP about alternative treatments such as ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, or inclisiran injections.
key_points: Total cholesterol levels above 7 or 7.5 may indicate familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), a genetic condition.
Dr Amir Khan advises patients who have tried three different statins without success to stop trying them.
Alternative treatments for high cholesterol include ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and inclisiran injections.
Many alternative treatments are now increasingly available directly through local GP surgeries.

title: Can Eating Tomatoes Reduce Liver Fat in Adults With MASLD?
author: Marilynn Larkin
content:
TOPLINE
Eating raw tomatoes and tomato sauce daily reduced the risk for hepatic steatosis in a small trial of adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
METHODOLOGY
- The researchers randomized 79 adults (median age, about 58 years; about 70% men) with MASLD and a BMI ≤ 30 to a tomato-rich diet (42 participants) or a tomato-free diet (37 participants) for 6 weeks.
- The intervention group ate 200 g of raw tomatoes and 50 g of tomato sauce daily; control individuals did not eat tomatoes in any form.
- The researchers measured liver fat using the FibroScan-based controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) at baseline and follow-up.
- Secondary outcomes included DEXA-measured body composition, liver stiffness, and metabolic and biochemical markers.
TAKEAWAY
- CAP decreased in both groups, with a significantly greater reduction in the intervention group (median change: -35.00 vs -18.00 dB/m), a difference that held after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI, and at follow-up.
- Hepatic steatosis reduction occurred without measurable changes in body composition or most metabolic and biochemical markers.
- At the trial end, body weight, BMI, waist circumference, and DEXA-measured fat mass did not differ significantly between groups.
- Liver stiffness, fibrosis scores, and metabolic markers such as glucose, lipids, and liver enzymes also did not differ significantly between groups.
IN PRACTICE
“These findings suggest that tomato consumption may reduce hepatic fat accumulation independently of major changes in body weight, total and abdominal adiposity, [and] support the potential role of tomato-based interventions as part of nutritional management for MASLD,” the authors of the study wrote.
SOURCE
The study was led by Rossella Tatoli of the National Institute of Gastroenterology IRCCS, Bari, Italy, and published online on July 30 in Nutrients.
LIMITATIONS
The study had several limitations. The sample size was small, the duration was short, and it was a single-center study. All participants had a BMI ≤ 30, so the results may not generalize to patients with obesity, who make up most MASLD cases in clinical practice. Adherence was self-reported. The study did not measure circulating lycopene or carotenoid levels, so the mechanism behind the hepatic steatosis reduction remains unclear.
DISCLOSURES
The authors declared no conflicts of interest.
summary: A small clinical trial found that a 6-week diet incorporating daily raw tomatoes and tomato sauce significantly reduced liver fat in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). The reduction in hepatic steatosis occurred independently of changes in body weight, fat mass, or most metabolic markers. Researchers noted limitations including a small sample size, short duration, and lack of generalizability to patients with obesity.
key_points: Participants on the tomato-rich diet consumed 200 g of raw tomatoes and 50 g of tomato sauce daily for 6 weeks.
Liver fat measured by CAP showed a significantly greater reduction in the tomato group compared to the control group.
The reduction in liver fat happened without measurable changes in body composition, waist circumference, or metabolic markers.
Study limitations included a small, single-center design, short duration, a participant BMI ≤ 30, and self-reported adherence.

title: Symptoms May Signal Prostate Cancer in Primary Care
author: Manasi Talwadekar
content:
TOPLINE
Men who presented to primary care with prostate symptoms had higher odds of a clinically significant prostate cancer diagnosis than those who underwent prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing, with no difference in stage.
METHODOLOGY
